en: Now,
having offered salutations to the self-existent Brahmā, the protector of the universe, and likewise to the seers of the mantras,
I desire to proclaim the ancient *Ṛgvidhāna*, which was previously seen by the ṛṣis who perceived the mantras.
From the mantras and from those who saw the mantras, according to the sequence of the traditional recitation,
Śaunaka proclaimed the ritual procedure for the rites perceived by the seers.
Rigveda 1.1.3ab: Various mantras were seen by the seers for various purposes;
they were prescribed for specific aims and demonstrated in their respective contexts.
The various ritual acts, which are based on pacification and nourishment,
as well as the spiritual accomplishments, have austerity as their root for one who performs them with faith.
RgV 1.1.(5a): Those modifications such as praise and so forth that have been taught, as well as the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) found in the *ṛks* and hymns; (5b):
listen now as they are being told those various desires by which the seers and the deities are praised.
Longevity, heaven, wealth, and sons—these four kinds of blessings are declared to be the primary objects of aspiration;
while hundreds of other desires have been prescribed by the sages and deities who offer praise.
RgV_1.2.(7a): When properly employed according to the rules, perfected mantras grant the fruit to a Brahmin.
RgV_1.2.(7b): Their means of accomplishment is truth, as well as self-restraint, tranquility, forbearance, freedom from envy, and control of the senses.
Therefore, a twice-born man, with a tranquil soul, devoted to silent recitation and burnt offerings,
should be intent upon austerity and study, showing compassion toward all living beings.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the prowess of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through silent recitation and burnt offerings.
Through austerity one attains heaven; through austerity one finds the Great.
For one whose self is restrained and who is joined with austerity, ritual actions succeed.
[Austerity brings about] incantations for causing enmity, for winning over others, for neutralizing poison, and for destroying disease.
By whichever seer and for whatever purpose each deity was praised.
RgV_1.3.(12a): Their various desires are fulfilled in those very ways;
RgV_1.3.(12b): I shall describe those diverse actions and the manifold varieties of karma.

Puraścaraṇa at the beginning of ritual acts brings about their successful accomplishment. At the outset of practicing the private recitation of the Veda, a twice-born man should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved off, bathed, and purified, he should remain standing during the day; at night, however, he should sit, remaining pure and restrained in speech.
One who speaks the truth should recite the purifiers (*pavitra*) as well as the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having recited those beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, one should likewise recite the *sāvitrī* and the verse beginning with "tat."
The hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha," the Śuddhavatīs, and the Aghamarṣaṇa; likewise the Śaṃvatīs, the Svastimatīs, and the Pāvamānīs.
RgV_1.4.(17a): This should be employed everywhere at the beginning and at the end of ritual actions.
RgV_1.4.(17b): One should recite it up to a thousand times, or up to a hundred, or ending with ten.

Having satiated with water the teacher, the seers, the meters, and the deities—reciting the syllable *oṃ*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* mantra, or else ten thousand times—RgV_1.4.(18). RgV_1.4.(18b).
One should approach Virūpākṣa while reciting the collection of fierce mantras;
one should not converse with non-Aryans, nor with Śūdras, nor with those who are censured.
RgV_1.4.(20a): Not with a woman who is menstruating, nor with outcasts, nor with men of the lowest castes;
RgV_1.4.(20b): nor with those who hate the gods or Brahmins, nor with those who revile their teachers or gurus.
One should not despise anyone who is hated by one's mother or father;
one should be devoted to auspicious conduct, approaching the waters three times a day.
At the end of the twelve nights, one should prepare a sthālīpāka (cooked offering in a pot) for Agni,
for Soma, and a third portion for both of them together.
Then, to the north, one should offer oblations to the Viśvedevas and to Rudra;
likewise, to the Lord of the Dwelling Place and also to Anumati.
RgV 1.5.24a: Another [verse] is addressed to Dhanvantari; there are also [verses] for the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
RgV 1.5.24b: The tenth is dedicated to Brāhmaṇaspati, while the following one is recorded as being for Brahmán.
RgV_1.5.(25a): Likewise, there are oblations for Sarasvatī and Viṣṇu, and the final one is for Sviṣṭakṛt.
RgV_1.5.(25b): These are indeed the clarified butter (ājya) oblations at the beginning; then, once the sthālīpāka has been offered, [the others follow].
Having offered oblations into the fire, he should satisfy the Brahmins; being pure and restrained in speech, he should eat.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, being pure and restrained in speech, he should eat the remainder.
The procedure for all the *kṛcchra* penances has been declared in due order:
that of the *prājāpatya*, the *atikṛcchra*, and likewise the *sāṃtapana*.
By the performance of the Parāka, the Kṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances,
one attains purification through one, and is liberated from sins through two.
By three [recitations], the mantras are perfected and one is released from minor offenses (*upapātaka*);
by four, one is likewise freed from the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*) and from officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice (*ayājya-yājana*).
By means of the five great sins and all evil deeds, one is completely liberated;
by the *taptakṛcchra* penance, one wards off all sins.
The Cāndrāyaṇa penance, together with its beginning and end, is considered equal to these Kṛcchra penances.
Purified by three Cāndrāyaṇas, one attains the world of Brahmā.
By means of eight [verses], one may directly behold the deities who grant boons;
likewise, by knowing the meters through ten [verses], one attains all desires.
For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days he should eat food obtained by begging;
for another three days he should not eat at all—this is the *prājāpatya* penance performed by a twice-born man.
A twice-born man performing the *atikṛcchra* penance should eat only a single mouthful for three sets of three days as previously described,
and he should fast for the final three days.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with fasting for one night— this is known as the *Sāṃtapanakṛcchra*.
They know this very [penance] joined with three-day periods as the Mahāsāṃtapana;
however, a fast for one hundred days is recorded as the Śiśusāṃtapana.
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air,
each for three days, bathing once a day and remaining composed.
If one drinks water while remaining restrained, it is recorded as the *prājāpatya* rule;
they call this the *yati-kṛcchra*, which removes all sins.
When one who is self-controlled and vigilant abstains from food for twelve days,
this penance called *parāka* removes all sins.
One should decrease the food by one morsel each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three sessions of the day, this is the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
One should perform this entire procedure during the middle [period] of the barley [month],
remaining disciplined from the beginning of the bright fortnight while practicing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A learned brahmin, having performed his daily rites, should eat four morsels in the morning;
and four when the sun has set—this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
With self-restraint, one should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food when midday has arrived;
this is the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
If one, being composed, eats three hundred and eighty morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever during a month, he attains the same world as the Moon.
The Rudras, as well as the Ādityas and the Vasus, observed this vow,
along with the Maruts together with the Ṛbhus, for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.

For seven nights, barley gruel should be drunk by one who has restrained his self; while reciting purifying prayers, he should observe the three daily ablutions and remain in standing or sitting postures.
When performed according to the rules, each single [verse] purifies one [of the seven bodily constituents] within seven nights:
the skin, blood, flesh, bone, fat, marrow, and even the vital essence.

Each of these [medicines] is a purifier of the skin and other bodily constituents for seven nights. Having purified his self through these observances, he should perform his ritual duties without sloth.
From that, one obtains all desired objects without a doubt;
among the three—grains, oil-cake, and buttermilk—each one individually serves as a purifier.
One whose self is purified, who speaks the truth, and who has conquered his senses, should perform ritual action.
Thus, I shall declare the rites for one who is purified by means of mantras, as follows.
One should fast for three nights at the outset of all ritual acts;
or alternatively, one may perform three nights of eating only at night, and thereafter commence the ritual act.
For those who perform [the sacrifice] regularly, there is a three-day vow at the beginning of the performance;
or one should fast afterwards, having performed the *sāmnipātika* [rite].
One should undertake those very rites that prolong life while joined with the mantras; one should mutter the *ṛc*-verses of the *trivṛt* hymn, which are auspicious and full of well-being.
And in the forest, when the sun has risen, having reached the unconquered quarter—
the east or the north— in a pure place, being composed in mind.
A twice-born man, having bathed in water with his clothes on and his head covered, and having sprinkled himself, should recite the *Śuddhavatī*,
the *Avatya*, the *Pāvamānī*, and the *Aghamarṣaṇa* verses.
Having thus immersed oneself three times and become pure, one should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
either three, six, eight, twelve, sixteen, or even eighteen times.

One should restrain the vital breaths while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* prayer until one hundred [breaths], or as long as there is satisfaction of the mind; for that long one should restrain the vital breaths.
In whatever measure his mind reproaches his evil deed,
in that same measure his body is released from that unrighteousness.
Having burned away his defects through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), wearing white garments and being pure,
he should sip water according to the rule and ascend the sacrificial grass mat (dharmaprastara).
Having placed his hands, with the *pavitra* blades, upon his lap, the right over the left;
having gazed at the space between the two directions and kept his eyes fixed without blinking.
Having mentally recited the syllable *oṃ*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*,
and the verse beginning with "tat," one should commence the beginning of the Veda.
One should recite softly in the morning, recite loudly at midday;
one should recite loudly in the afternoon, but cease during the time of twilight.
Rising during the Brāhma-muhūrta, the twice-born man should bathe three times and recite [the Veda],
adopting a moderate tempo— neither too fast nor too slow.
One should stand during the morning twilight reciting prayers and sit during the evening twilight;
one should not speak in between, nor should one cease in any way whatsoever.
When a Brāhmaṇa has arrived, one may cease [reciting] and converse with him as desired;
but upon seeing a Śūdra who has arrived, one should not recite under any circumstances.
The first hymn dedicated to Agni is indeed preeminent and esteemed by the brahmin seers; by reciting this auspicious hymn that bestows increase of wealth, a learned man shall attain his purpose.
Having recited this entire *Ṛṣi-sarva* along with its *puṭa*, being self-controlled and pure, one obtains the fruit of the *Ṛgveda Saṃhitā*; of this there is no doubt.
Chanting this eternal Brahman eleven times,
one attains all desires and is completely liberated from sins.
By reciting this *Saṃhitā* every single morning without eating,
one obtains long life, wealth, sons, and a healthy home.
While muttering this *brahman*, one should not look at Śūdras or others of that sort;
having looked [at them], one should sip water and, being purified, look at a cow, fire, or the sun.

The audible recitation (*japa*) is tenfold [in merit]; the whispered (*upāṃśu*) is a hundredfold; one should know that the mental (*mānasa*) is a thousandfold. This is remembered as the rule for recitation (*japya-vidhi*).
At the very beginning, one should perform the ritual with the Sāvitrī for the sake of peace;
for the sake of nourishment, the acquisition of wealth, the acquisition of cattle, and prosperity.
For this *nicṛt* verse, consisting of all the essence of the Veda, is commensurate with the Vedas;
it was seen through fierce asceticism by the wise Viśvāmitra.
One should always perform oblations and silent recitations as sacrifices with this [verse];
for the sake of the fulfillment of all desires, this is called the supreme Brahman.
This same [hymn], when recited in reverse order, verse by verse, destroys enemies;
this same [hymn], with its syllables in reverse order, is recommended for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
One should know that whatever ritual action is performed with this syllable, which is difficult to master, is unfailing; for this indeed is the power of Brahman.
One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks that cause obstruction, recited in reverse syllables,
using mustard oil with a ladle made of *vaibhītaka* wood.
He who desires the affliction of an enemy, or even his eradication,
should crush the enemies step by step and cause them to perish syllable by syllable.
RgV_1.16.(79a): Hereafter, I shall describe the ritual procedure for the first hymn of the Ṛgveda;
RgV_1.16.(79b): according to how the seer Madhucchandas performed this rite in former times.
Restrained, he should carry fire upon his head for a full year,
eating as his sacrificial oblation the remains of the offering at every fourth mealtime.
Offering oblations, one who speaks the truth should worship [the fire] three times every day. When the time for the vow has arrived, he should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) dedicated to Agni.
Even if fire is meditated upon where there is no physical fire, that fire stands before him at the conclusion of his vow.
If he should desire, "May I burn this," the purifier indeed burns it.
Even in the waters, fire blazes forth; such is the power of the great-souled one's vow.
And the Fire-god, through diligent effort, fulfills him with his desired objects.
Beyond this, there are seven triplets (ṛcas) beginning with Vāyu which have been proclaimed;
by reciting them constantly with self-restraint, one attains all desired objects.
In the case of the seer Medhātithi, one should [recite] the verse beginning with "sadasas patim.
One desiring wisdom should constantly mutter this [verse] and offer clarified butter as an oblation with it.
Having bathed and become pure, the wise man should daily recite the verse beginning with "syonā" (O Earth, be pleasant) over the earth;
he thereby obtains a vast territory, free from rivals and thorns.
With these five verses beginning with "This [Viṣṇu]" (RgV 1.17), one should perform the Śrāddha rite;
by immersing the thumb into the food, one thereby repels the Rākṣasas.
Having committed sins spanning seven lifetimes, as well as the eating of forbidden food,
one becomes purified by reciting "tad viṣṇoḥ" once while standing in the midst of water.
The hymn beginning with "The mothers come" (ambayo yanti), which consists of nine verses, is prescribed for consecration;
it is proclaimed to be life-prolonging, medicinal, and a liberator from evil.
If the seer Śunaḥśepa, while bound or imprisoned, were to recite this, he would be released from all fetters; even one who is diseased would become free from disease.
He who desires to obtain eternal boons from Indra,
the destroyer of cities, should praise Indra with these very sixteen verses day after day.
The hymn of Indra beginning with *hairaṇyastūpa* is a praise of his deeds;
by reciting it with self-restraint, one repels enemies without effort.
He who constantly worships the Sun with the Ṛgvedic verse beginning "With the black [ray]" (ākṛṣṇena) shall live free from disease and in happiness— at dawn, at midday, or even at sunset.
Meditating upon this single verse, "ākṛṣṇena," day and night,
one who offers clarified butter into the fire with it shall obtain a long life.
A traveler should recite this Sāvitrī verse beginning with "ye te panthāḥ";
he will travel his path in safety and reach his home unharmed.
The hymn beginning with "O Pūṣan" which the seer Kaṇva, the son of Ghora, sang—
this should be understood as a means for removing highway robbers while on a journey.
Whoever should praise Īśāna day after day with the six verses addressed to Rudra,
that person shall always obtain peace for women, men, and cattle from Śaṅkara.
With this very hymn of six verses, one should offer clarified butter daily;
or, desiring prosperity, one should prepare an oblation of cooked rice for Rudra on the festival days.
Day after day, one should worship the rising sun with the verse beginning "ud.
For this indeed destroys heart disease and increases supreme health.
The half-verse beginning with "dviṣantam" (the hater)—one should recite this while meditating upon whoever one hates. By doing so for seven nights, the wrongdoer incurs enmity.
Whether seized by diseases or free from them, one should recite the excellent third triplet of Praskaṇva (RgV 1.19).
One who is self-restrained should constantly mutter this [hymn] for the sake of health many times.
The latter half-verse of that [hymn] is known as "dviṣad dveṣa" (the hater-hating).
Having seen one whom he hates, he should meditate upon him and mutter this [verse].
If one who has committed an offense recites [this] for three nights, he subdues enmity;
by reciting it at midday, he causes inexhaustible life and splendor to arise.
When the sun has set, it repels the hater;
thus, vigor, splendor, health, and the hatred of the enemy are proclaimed.
The hymns beginning with "nava paśva," which Parāśara [saw] while in the womb—
these take away the life-breaths of enemies and bring them under one's control.
One desiring sons, cattle, wealth, heaven, long life, and freedom from blindness should study the eleven purifying hymns (*sūkta*) of Suparṇa.
One who is well-composed through the recitation of these internal verses shall attain the supreme abode,
the eternal light of the universe.
The sage who recites the *Ānuṣṭubha*, the *Āyuṣya*, and the *Vaiśvadeva* hymns—
even if he is on the verge of death— shall attain a full lifespan by reciting these.
At the time of the śrāddha for the ancestors, one should recite these three verses beginning with "madhu.
The ancestors of that person, becoming non-terrible (aghorāḥ), enter into the supreme light.
One should gaze upon the risen moon with the hymn beginning "Thou, O Soma" (RgV 1.91).
Month after month, one should worship it with fuel in hand, offering fresh [oblations] each time.
Indeed, for that month, his threefold suffering shall never occur;
this destruction of one's own death was formerly seen by Gotama.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship him as he rises and likewise when he is full;
by this, one may obtain garments and attain the same world as the Moon.
One who desires wealth should constantly recite these [verses] perpetually;
having bathed, being pure and self-restrained, one shall obtain the desired wealth.

One desiring long life should constantly recite this hymn of Kutsa, beginning with "imam" (Ṛgveda 1.22). Being pure and restrained in speech, one should also offer oblations of clarified butter, reciting it verse by verse.
Having bathed and being self-restrained, one should recite [the hymn] "apa naḥ śośucat" at midday when the sun is shining; thus he shall directly cross over calamity.
One who desires purification, being restrained in diet, should offer clarified butter with each verse; or he may offer eight fuel-sticks daily, for this hymn is the destroyer of sin.
Just as the inner core of the muñja grass is extracted [from its sheaths], so is one released from evil.
One should constantly recite the hymn beginning with "jātavedase" for the sake of securing well-being.
For one who has set out on a difficult path, there shall be no fear of enemies; nor, whether engaged in royal service or with a herd of horses, shall he have fear even if accused in many ways.
When faced with an impossible task, a sudden inspiration, or even a danger that threatens one's life,
by muttering this verse beginning with "jātavedase," one is liberated from those [perils].
One who has set out desiring to accomplish a goal should mutter this in his mind; having accomplished his purpose, he returns in safety and shall not perish on the way.
Having accomplished his purpose, while returning to his own home, he should always practice this very [mantra]. He should likewise recite it when the sun has risen and when it has set.
One should always recite this hymn, which destroys bad dreams, at dawn as a blessing for the day, and at nightfall as a blessing for the night, when the light has broken.

RgV 1.23 (123a): While in labor, one should mutter the verse beginning with "pramandinaḥ"; it is the "liberator of the fetus. RgV 1.23 (123b): And the woman should meditate upon Indra in her mind; thus she releases the fetus.
In times of distress, or when desiring all things, one should constantly recite the Ṛṣi Trita;
having bathed, one should recite the seven [verses] beginning with "indrā" for the Vaiśvadeva rite.
He who offers clarified butter is released from all distress;
this final hymn, consisting of twenty-five verses, is the most excellent, known as the *Śāntātīya*.
Having paid homage to the two Nāsatyas, one shall attain supreme prosperity;
this hymn is a praise of Dharma and a liberation from sin.
A twice-born man, being pure, should constantly mutter this "Imā" hymn, which is addressed to Rudra;
he obtains long life, knowledge, wealth, sons, and a healthy home.

Having fasted for three nights and being pure, one should [recite] the two hymns beginning with "mā no mahāntam" (RV 1.24) to remove from oneself the taint of evil dreams regarding heroes, offspring, or cattle-pens.
One should offer oblations of *audumbara* wood, prepared with curds, honey, and clarified butter;
one should offer clarified butter with the hymn at the beginning and at the end of the ritual acts.
Having praised Bhava a hundred times with the hymn while raising his arms,
one shall cut all the bonds of death and live free from diseases.
Standing with fuel in hand, always pure, one should worship the rising sun with this hymn, beginning with the verse "citram. (RgV 1.24)
By constantly praising the Sun at midday with this hymn,
one drives away evil and attains both wealth and long life.
One should recite "adhaḥsvapnasya" every single morning, day after day;
it quickly dispels bad dreams, and one has no fear of hunger.
"Both I purify"—thus [the verse] is proclaimed as the "slayer of enemies. By reciting these, one slays the *rakṣases* and subdues one's rivals.
Having performed the five sacrifices, offered oblations into the fire, and completed his daily rites,
one who recites these divine verses shall obtain all desires.
Having paid homage to Indra and Viṣṇu with the three verses beginning with "viṣṇor nu kam," one should,
with fuel in hand and having become pure, perform worship day after day.
One attains righteousness, intelligence, wealth, sons, health, and the increase of sacred knowledge;
and one reaches the supreme, eternal station whose form is light.
Seeing an assassin approaching, or a tiger, or even a wolf,
one is released from them by muttering the mantra "na mā garan" (may they not devour me).
Having fasted for three nights, one should recite [the hymn] at night until the sun appears. Having bathed and become pure, one should worship the Sun, the maker of day, with the solar verses.
Thieves and others of evil conduct do not see him;
traveling alone on the road, he may protect himself from hundreds of robbers.
Having committed theft through delusion, a twice-born man becomes pure by fasting for three nights;
by reciting the *Asya Vāmīya* hymn, he shall quickly be released from that sin.
He who, though surrounded by kinsmen, sons, friends, and allies, still desires to rule a kingdom,
should remain constantly self-restrained and recite this hymn mentally.
Having committed slander against his teacher, the king, and the twice-born with the hymn beginning "kayā śubhā," Śaunaka, having heard the secret of another, spoke even against his own guru.
One who is self-restrained should mutter these two verses beginning with "imam nu somam" (RgV 1.26).
He shall obtain all his desires, and no sin whatsoever shall remain.
One should always perform the ritual worship with the hymn *pitum nu* so that food is constantly present;
one should always honor the food and eat it without disparaging it.
No disease born of food shall befall him, nor shall even poison turn into food. Having drunk poison, one should mutter this hymn, which is the destroyer of poison.
One should not eat while speaking, nor while impure, nor when the food is loathsome; rather, one who is always pure should give, honor, and offer oblations.
He shall have no fear of hunger whatsoever, nor shall he suffer from any disease born of lack of food;
even one who has set out on a wrong path or has strayed from the path at any point [shall find safety].
One who has set out upon a wrong path, or having performed a censurable deed,
should offer clarified butter with each verse of the hymn beginning "O Agni, lead us" (agnē naya).
Chanting [the hymns] while constantly restrained, he should worship the Fire;
having bathed, he should mutter the *anarvāṇam* [hymn], having paid homage to Bṛhaspati.
One obtains heroes and wealth, and attains great renown;
one who is afflicted by poison should recite with self-restraint this hymn beginning with "kaṅkato na."
Poison does not affect him, even from a serpent or from the venom of a gaze; nor does the poison found in insects and spiders, nor that which is produced by fanged creatures or scorpions.
By reciting both the original and the composed [mantras], one dispels everything:
dharma, intelligence, wealth, sons, good fortune, and spiritual luster.
Health, nourishment, long life, cattle, knowledge, and great fame—
[may these be attained] by one who has fasted for three nights, bathed, purified, and observed the vow.
Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should worship the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices (Śatakratu) for one day,
with feet joined together by a razor, and speech restrained.
Recalling the seer Gṛtsamada with the hymn beginning "yo jāta" (RgV 2.12),
one should recite this [hymn] a hundred times, and at the end, the verse beginning "indra śreṣṭha" (RgV 8.97.1).
In one day he obtains wealth; in two days, unsurpassed success;
in three days, health; and in four days, abundant food.
With five [verses], one gains spiritual luster; with six, one brings about long life and happiness;
with seven, one obtains offspring; and with eight, one attains prosperity and fame.
He becomes dear to Indra and attains his beloved abode;
he is the slayer of enemies, the subduer of Dasyus, and the supreme bringer of wealth.
One should mutter the hymn beginning with "gaṇānām," which increases happiness;
being self-restrained, one should always mutter this [hymn] addressed to Bṛhaspati at the two twilights.
One should worship with this hymn for the fulfillment of all desires;
and [one should recite] this verse beginning with "O King, he who to me... (RgV 1.24.11), which pacifies bad dreams.
Having recited this, a pure Brāhmaṇa who is the best among those who know the Veda, being self-restrained and having fasted for one day and night, quickly destroys an evil dream.
For the sake of progeny, one should offer clarified butter or rice cooked in milk with the five verses beginning with "rākā mahaḥ" on the sixth day of the bright fortnight.
Having himself consumed the remainder of the oblation, one obtains great progeny;
even he who may be overcome by a terrible, life-taking disease.

Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one who is pure and restrained in speech should offer a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with a single verse from the *raudra* hymn, reciting it verse by verse.
Having first offered oblations of clarified butter and then paid homage to Śaṅkara,
he should subsist on the remnants of the sacrificial offering, remaining vigilant and taking a single meal at intervals.
On the full moon day, one should recite [this hymn]; one shall be liberated from death and diseases.
Even if one has been falsely accused out of delusion, or has performed a censurable act, [by this recitation] one is purified.
Having bathed and eaten, one should recite without weariness the verse beginning with "Amba" while in the water.
Furthermore, he who sets out on a journey and sees a bird taking flight—
Whether the situation be unfavorable or favorable, one should remain composed, look upon it, and recite with self-restraint;
one should worship with the two hymns beginning with "kanikradat," pronouncing the correct accents.
Whether it be a bird, a crow, or even a fanged beast,
one should recite this mantra for bewildering thieves even without seeing them.
Whether it be a bird of auspicious call or another that neither cries out nor is seen—
One should indeed recite [the mantra] after having paid homage; once the purpose is accomplished, one should withdraw.
For him there is no fear whatsoever from robbers, whether on a road or anywhere else;
he crosses over even difficult passages, and being possessed of well-being, he shall be happy.
He whose food is neither digested nor remains in any way [undigested], having meditated upon the eater of that food, should mutter the *ṛc*: "I am Agni. (RgV_2.1.3ab)
One should recite the dialogue of Viśvāmitra regarding the crossing of rivers from the Ṛgveda 2.1.4a. Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, one should cast a handful of water.
The rivers protect with their currents that man who constantly practices this [verse], "Homage to those who flow," just as mothers protect their own son.
And no fear exists for him, even among those who dwell on riverbanks;
he is not afflicted by cold or heat from beings that move in the water.
One who wishes to cross a full river should remember the words, "Rest yourselves! (RgV 2.2.7a).
Furthermore, one who is crossing a river should mutter the verse beginning with "O, yes" (o sv iti) while in the midst of the waters (RgV 2.2.7b).
That twice-born man quickly reaches the shore or finds firm ground,
just as one who desires to cross to the further bank of the waters swiftly does so with a well-yoked chariot.
One who is self-restrained should personally mutter this verse, "ud va ūrmiḥ";
likewise, one setting out on a journey should recollect the verse beginning with "ā mandraiḥ."
Having completed all his duties without exception, he indeed returns again to his home;
[he does so] toward one who never gives for the sake of well-being, whose consciousness is always possessed [by greed].
Having killed him, one should seek that wealth while recollecting, "What do they do for you?
The hymn beginning with "Indrā parvatā" is remembered as bestowing long life and wealth.
He who, being deluded regarding the organ of speech, does not attain true knowledge;
or he who, in any way whatsoever, does not understand either the objects of the senses or other [higher] objects.
If the knowledge that has been acquired by someone should perish again and again, he should recite the two *sasarparī* verses for two months; thus he regains it.
One should remember that when the oxen are steady, he travels with the cart;
with four steady followers, the skilled man goes forth having achieved his purpose.
Seeing the axle of a vehicle broken at its end on a difficult road,
a twice-born man should recite the two verses beginning with "abhi vyayasva," bestowing strength upon the axle.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for three nights and being pure,
one should stand in a cemetery situated on ground sloping toward the south, with a concentrated mind.
Rigveda 2.4.17ab: He who wears a red turban, has blood on his hands, carries fuel from the Bilva tree, and eats blue food—[for him] one should offer sesame oil mixed with salt for seven days.

RgV_2.4.(18a): Reciting the *samidh* verses of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree while addressing the enemies of Vasiṣṭha; RgV_2.4.(18b): having fashioned an image of the one whom he hates out of *śamyāka* wood at night.
And having presided over that [rite], the twice-born should perform it with four *ṛc* verses;
this oblation, performed while uttering the [victim's] name, ensures that he does not live for seven nights.
This Brahman, uttered by the Kuśikas, slays the Vasiṣṭhas from their very roots;
for one who mutters it or offers oblations with it, there is nothing that cannot be slain.

One should recite twenty-two times this unsurpassed hymn concerning the inner self; by doing so constantly with self-restraint on the festival days of the moon's phases, one attains all desired objects.
Bṛhaspati, Aja-ekapād, Savitṛ, and Babhru—
the two who increase the cosmic order (Ṛtāvṛdhau)— [one should worship] day after day with five triplets (ṛcas) every successive day.

One should offer clarified butter, verse by verse, with the five verses beginning "O Bṛhaspati" (RgV 2.5). Having offered the oblation and having worshipped the fire with perfumes, garlands, and incense.
They worship those very five deities with fivefold desires:
with jewels, offspring, cattle, sacrifices, and long life.
Now, I shall fully expound the procedure for generating grace from the Gītā of the Vedas and other scriptures—
the Gāyatrī mantra— which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
In the triad of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, the Gāyatrī is the ultimate refuge;
indeed, there is nothing superior to the Gāyatrī in this world and in the next.

Eating pure food in moderation, observing silence, and intent upon bathing three times a day and performing worship, the wise man, with his mental activity focused on nothing else, should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times.
Thereafter, he should engage him in ritual acts either sequentially or according to his own desire.
As long as he performs the task, he must not neglect that vow.
Having bathed at sunrise, one should recite [the hymn] a thousand times every day;
one will certainly obtain long life, health, sovereignty, and wealth.
Having fasted for three nights and properly offered ghee a thousand times into a fire fed with fuel-sticks of khadira wood, one obtains a thousandfold gain.
By offering fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood smeared with clarified butter into the sacrificial fire at the conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun, one obtains a thousandfold gain.
Having offered red sandalwood mixed with ghee into a fire made of khadira wood,
one obtains the merit of performing a thousand oblations during the conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun.
Having offered cow-dung mixed with red sandalwood and clarified butter into the fire,
a twice-born man obtains a thousand cattle as wealth.
Having offered into the fire thousands of pellets made from the dung of that cow,
smeared with ghee, one obtains that very cow.
With barley one obtains horses, with sesame seeds elephants, and likewise with barley-gruel (yāvaka) one obtains buffalo-cows;
by an oblation of rice and husked grain, one shall obtain a daughter.
By offering thousands of *jāti*, *campaka*, *rāja-arika*, and *arka* flowers,
smeared with clarified butter, into the fire, one obtains garments.
Having offered water by the thousands into the solar disc or into the midst of water, one obtains a thousand gold pieces;
if it is offered into the lunar disc, one obtains a thousand silver pieces.
He who bathes with water over which the mantra has been recited a thousand times shall be liberated from misfortune, sin, impurity, disease, and obstacles.
In whichever direction one scatters a clod of earth while reciting [the mantra] seven times,
fears arising from thieves, fire, or wind shall certainly not occur.
RgV_2.9.(40a): Subsisting on milk, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; thus one wards off untimely death.
RgV_2.10.(40b): Consuming ghee, one shall obtain a pure accumulation of vast knowledge.

Having offered leaves of the *vetasa* tree smeared with clarified butter into the sacrificial fire, one shall cause the god to rain for a hundred thousand years; he will become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, without a doubt.
By a hundred thousand oblations of ashes, even a *kṛtyā* (sorcery) rises up from the water;
standing facing the sun in pure water reaching to the navel, one becomes purified.
By offering a hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter into the fire,
one whose self is fulfilled by all desires shall attain supreme perfection.
By offering a hundred thousand oblations of barley grains smeared with clarified butter into the consumer of oblations,
one whose self is fulfilled by all desires shall attain the supreme station.
By means of a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter, one shall obtain all desires;
by reciting [the mantra] a hundred thousand times while subsisting on the five products of the cow, one shall become a rememberer of past births.
Indeed, by offering that very [oblation] into the fire, one obtains abundant wealth;
and by the constant offering of food, one shall always possess an abundance of food.
One should offer oblations ten thousand times for all those things to be accomplished.
By offering oblations for the sake of red-colored perfected ones, one subdues all enemies.
By offering salt mixed with honey, one shall bring all under control;
by offering blood from heroic men accompanied by the sound "hu," one shall produce fever.
Having offered oil from the *vibhītaka* tree, one should drive [the enemy] away from the very place;
but having offered *nimba* leaves, one shall produce enmity among men.
By offering red rice grains smeared with clarified butter into the consumer of oblations,
one obtains strength and is not conquered by enemies.
For the sake of accomplishing the bringing back [of the cow],
as he offered cow's milk mixed with honey and clarified butter into the blazing fire, that [fire] was extinguished.
He who, as a celibate student (brahmacārī) with moderate food, recites [this] three thousand times, shall obtain wealth and sovereignty within a year; of this there is no doubt.
By offering oblations of flowers and sacrificial fuel-sticks from the *śamī*, *bilva*, and *palāśa* trees— and especially those of the *arka*— one shall obtain gold.
If one takes refuge in the abode of him who [is the lord] of Abrahma, Tryambaka, and the others,
and recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while abstaining from food, he shall become a granter of boons to that person.
By offering one hundred thousand *bilva* fruits smeared with clarified butter into the sacrificial fire,
one attains supreme prosperity, provided that one has not been a killer of an embryo.
By offering a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with ghee into the sacrificial fire,
one obtains an entire kingdom that is free from rivals and thorns.
By reciting twenty-five hundred thousand [times] while subsisting on curd, milk, and ghee,
a person achieves success in their own body, according to the doctrine of Kauśika.
For one day I subsisted on the five products of the cow, for one day I fed on air;
for one day I ate the food of a Brāhmaṇa—this is called the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Having bathed with a hundred *gāyatrī* verses, one should mutter [the verse] a hundred times while submerged within the water;
then, having drunk water a hundred times, one is liberated from all sins.

The killer of a cow, the killer of a father, the killer of a mother, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the Guru’s bed, the stealer of gold and jewels, and that Brahmin who drinks liquor— [these are all purified by this].
Having performed the officiation of a sacrifice for one unworthy of sacrificing, or having committed a censurable act,
one does not perish even by accepting as a gift the entire earth together with its oceans.
And those planets such as the Sun and others that are ill-disposed toward him in this world on earth—they all become gentle and auspicious; of this there is no doubt.
Reciting the hymn beginning with "kṛṇuṣva," which destroys demons, while surrounded by enemies,
one shall take away the life-breaths of the hostile ones and utterly destroy even the *rakṣas* spirits.
Whoever worships the Fire day after day with the verse beginning "pari," him the Fire himself protects on every side, he whose face is turned everywhere.
Whoever constantly worships Śakra with the hymn beginning "ko adya" (RgV 2.12),
or recites it with salutations, obtains boons from Śakra.
One should perform a rite for well-being at night with the Vāmadevya hymn beginning with "kayā" (RV 4.31).
Or, one should recite this Brahman-hymn uttered by the Kuśikas during the periods of twilight.
With the verse beginning "The swan dwelling in purity," one should gaze at the sun with a pure mind;
chanting it at the time of death, one goes to the eternal abode of Brahman.
When undertaking agriculture,
however, one should offer a cooked mess of grain (sthālīpāka) according to the rules in the middle of the field with five [verses] beginning with "śunam vāhāḥ."
Just as a plowman directs his plow according to the marks [of the soil],
so [should one direct it] for Indra, for the Maruts, for Parjanya, and for Bhaga.
Having offered oblations to Pūṣan for the grain, to Sītā for the furrow, and then further to Śunaḥsīra,
one should sacrifice separately to these deities as well.
With offerings of perfumes, garlands, fruits, parched grain, wine, and spirits;
at the time of sowing, reaping, threshing, and the preparation of the furrows.
One who is pure should always worship these very deities according to the prescribed ritual;
thus his action becomes unfailing, and his cultivation always prospers.
One should mutter this three-verse hymn addressed to Kṣetrapati, beginning with "Of the field's lord" (RgV 2.14).
A twice-born man who constantly gazes upon the sun obtains the most excellent field.
One should worship mice with this *caru* offering upon heaps of mouse-droppings;
and one should always praise the lord of mice with the verse beginning "O Citraratha, King! (RgV 2.14.3).
At this time, one should feed the Brahmins and also feed the plowmen;
being vigilant and devoted to peace, one should personally engage in agriculture.
The destruction of land, the harming of cattle, and the destruction of grass, insects, and so forth—
the sin committed in these cases is purified by the gift to a wicked person.
One should present a twentieth part of the grain to those learned in the Vedas;
for by the gift of that twentieth part, one is released from the defects of agriculture.
He who should always offer clarified butter with the hymn beginning "From the ocean" (RgV 2.15),
according to the very ritual procedure previously described, being self-restrained and having conquered his senses;
With the mantra "vi jyotiṣā," one should cause the fire to blaze wherever one desires in the Jātavedas;
Agni protects that person on all sides with auspicious wealth.
He who worships Vahni with these two verses beginning with "viśvāni na" overcomes all calamities and attains imperishable glory.

Having offered oblations with the hymn beginning "O Agni, you... (RgV 3.20), one who desires wealth and long life should remain in the form of the fire as the carrier of oblations for the sake of the vital breaths.
He who desires various kinds of wealth and incomparable,
great strength should worship the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices with the hymn beginning with "Uroṣṭha."
One who desires offspring should constantly sacrifice with *caru* to the wives of the gods;
having presented the offering, he should eat the remainder while restraining his speech.
RgV_2.16.(84a): And the remains of the offering should be given to his wife by one desiring a son.
RgV_2.16.(84b): He should prepare the sacrificial porridge with the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same color.
One quickly obtains offspring worthy of oneself; there is no doubt about this.
A twice-born man, being pure, should daily recite the *Svasthyātreyī* every morning.
This auspicious hymn is meritorious and destroys all impurities;
one should recite it over a friend or a kinsman as they depart.
Having uttered the words "A path of well-being," one travels the road with well-being;
"Be parted, O Lord of the Forest"—this is known as the *cyāvana* [charm].
If one should desire to cause someone to fall, one should cause them to fall while reciting this [hymn].
Or, having stepped with one's foot upon an image made of dust on the ground, one should [act] against the hater.
As if about to turn back from battle, he does not waver; of this there is no doubt.
Or, one should cause a woman who has fainted during childbirth to drink [the water] consecrated with this mantra.
By means of the *udakacyāvana* [rite], the fetus is easily brought down.
One who desires rain should employ the hymn beginning with "acchāvada. (RgV 2.17)
If one remains without food and wears worn-out clothes, it will rain before long,
provided that ten thousand oblations of cane-wood sticks smeared with milk have been offered into the fire.
He who desires that the boon-granting Goddess Śrī may dwell eternally in his family shall obtain great rain by reciting this hymn with a covering invocation.
Having become pure and self-restrained, one should offer clarified butter daily;
and one desiring prosperity should constantly recite the fifteen-verse hymn dedicated to Śrī.
One should invoke Śrī upon a lotus with five [verses], or [upon] gold;
one should present white offerings, such as food and milk and curd.
One should prepare a dish of boiled rice with milk;
then, having purified oneself through the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, one should approach Śrī with self-restraint.

Having bathed with all kinds of herbs, with decoctions, and with purifying waters, let the consecration for the king be performed with the mantra: "May the friend of the gods come to me. (RgV 2.18.96ab)
"Manasaḥ kāmam" (RgV 2.18.1)—this [verse] is for one desiring cattle at the consecration ceremony;
"kadarmeṇa" (RgV 2.18.2)—with this, he who is pure in his vows and desiring offspring should bathe.
One who desires sovereignty, being pure and firm in his vows, should bathe while reciting "aśvapūrṇām";
a Brāhmaṇa, however, should bathe on a red hide according to the prescribed rule.
The Kṣatriya king [should sit] upon a tiger skin, while the Vaiśya [sits] upon a goat skin;
immediately thereafter, the oblation (homa) should be performed.
A twice-born man should offer lotuses with clarified butter while reciting "candrām";
by the verse beginning with "ādityavarṇa," the oblation of bilva fruits is prescribed.
Or rather, the twice-born man may have fire with *bilva* wood as fuel and offer oblations from a cooking pot;
a sacrifice of ten thousand [oblations] performed by one desiring prosperity is the first rule.
Having offered ten million oblations correctly, one obtains infinite prosperity;
and having offered ten thousand oblations with clarified butter, one obtains it a hundredfold.
One attains infinite, uninterrupted, and eternal prosperity.
For one who is unable [to perform the ritual], the recitation (*japa*) of ten thousand [verses] is declared to be the superior alternative.
Having properly recited it ten thousand times, one obtains infinite glory;
indeed, by reciting it a hundred times ten thousand times, one enjoys prosperity.
One should constantly offer lotuses by the thousands into the waters at night;
having seen the Goddess Śrī, one should indeed cease [the practice], for one truly fears being afflicted with leprosy.
One who subsists on *bilva* fruits and dwells in a *bilva* grove should offer *bilva* fruits with clarified butter;
within twenty-one nights, he attains supreme perfection.
With whatever desire one offers oblations with self-restraint for the sake of prosperity— whether it be lotuses or even bilva fruits— that very desire is fulfilled.
One should never summon prosperity for the sake of a miser;
nor should an oblation ever be performed out of a desire for anything whatsoever.
Whether seeking great things, or desiring sovereignty once more,
one who strives to attain the supreme speech should worship Śrī with diligent effort.
One should offer clarified butter daily with the hymn beginning "Agni shall come" (Ṛgveda 2.21);
thereby one obtains powerful, righteous, and auspicious offspring.
With the verse beginning "Acchā na," one should worship the radiant Vibhāvasu;
having obtained progeny, he shall conquer his enemies and cross over all difficulties.
One who desires that those cows— the mothers of the world— be always inexhaustible should worship them with the hymn beginning "ā gāvaḥ" while they are in the cow-pen or as they are departing.
One should worship the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices with the *pragātha* hymn beginning "tvām id dhi" (RgV 8.69.2);
by reciting it at midday and during both twilights, one shall obtain wealth.
With the three verses beginning with "upa," one should touch the king's drums in battle;
he thereby acquires vigor and strength and brings his enemies under control.

He who, taking a blade of grass in his hand, practices the recitation "This is a sacrifice, this is not a sacrifice," obtains the fruit of having studied this hymn; one who does not take the grass does not.

And at the end of the hymn, one should carefully cast a blade of grass into the fire, or into a barren spot, or even into water; having abandoned it there, one should go elsewhere, for [otherwise] it brings fear.
Holding grass in his hand and reciting the hymn that slays demons, even when surrounded by Dasyus,
he encounters no fear whatsoever from either demons or enemies.
But one who departs from his home with the desire for wealth, while traveling on the road,
should diligently recite the *pathyā* verse as he proceeds along the path.
Meditating upon this very verse, "ye ke ca jmā," day and night,
and having offered clarified butter into the fire with it, one shall obtain a long life.
The hymn beginning with "vayam u tvā" (RgV 2.23) is dedicated to Pūṣan; it increases one's wealth. Having become pure, one should recite it constantly, and one obtains the desired riches.
O Sampūṣan, he whose property— be it cattle, bipeds, or wealth— has been lost,
or who has lost it on the road through delusion, should recite [this hymn] at night.
A twice-born man, having become pure, should constantly recite this hymn to Sarasvatī, beginning with "iyam" and ending with "antam"; he becomes eloquent and wise.
That hymn of yours which consists of eight verses and is known as being in the *triṣṭubh* meter—
by constantly reciting it with a restrained mind, one attains all desired objects.
That hymn which was produced by the shatterer of mountains is a destroyer of rivals.
Having paid homage to Bṛhaspati, one lays low many enemies.
Whether one is guilty of sin, or falsely accused, or having committed a censurable deed,
by reciting the entire *Soma-raudra* hymn, he removes all guilt.
Or, he who, constantly observing the vow of clarified butter, should offer oblations with these verses,
shall be released from the nooses of Varuṇa and likewise obtain peace.
Having observed the ritual procedure for the hymn to the clouds according to its specific characteristics,
one should perform the rites with the *ṛc* verses of the chariot parts according to the prescribed rule.
One should employ this [rite] for a king who is about to set out for battle;
he should consecrate all his limbs, his chariot-horses, and his excellent steeds with mantras.
To whatever place he may go, even against an enemy, when consecrated with this mantra, he shall not return without having conquered; for the power of the Brahman is supreme.
He who desires sons, long life, health, and imperishable happiness,
that man should offer clarified butter daily with the hymn beginning "agnim naro."
One should begin the recitation at the two twilights with three hymns beginning with "pra agnaye. Such a person knows no fear from demons and obtains inexhaustible wealth.
He who constantly honors you with the *pragātha* hymn, O Vrajin,
enjoys abundant prosperity and attains both wealth and long life.
One should constantly recite these [verses]: "śaṃvatīḥ" and "śam na indrāgnī. Through this, there shall be no fear from demons, nor from malevolent spirits, nor from diseases.
One who desires to marry and is afflicted by disease should constantly practice the Bhaga-sūkta;
he quickly finds a marriage and is liberated from his ailments.
A twice-born man, being pure, should daily recite the *raudra-sūkta* beginning with "imāḥ";
by reciting it, he himself is not harmed in terms of progeny or wealth.
But he who, wishing to cross the waters at the confluence of rivers,
should mutter this hymn that begins with "The ocean is the eldest," it removes all fear.
In the hymn dedicated to Āditya, which slays enemies and destroys diseases, one who has become pure should recite it in the morning; thus, one is liberated from enemies and diseases.
One should mutter this hymn dedicated to Vāstoṣpati, beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling, come back" (RgV 7.54).
Having bathed and performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, this supreme Brahman is now being declared.
With the hymn beginning "amīvahā" (RgV 2.26), one should lull all beings to sleep at night;
for indeed, no other means of inducing sleep is found anywhere like this.
Whether in a narrow pass, on uneven ground, or in a difficult terrain; whether bound or having escaped somewhere;
whether fleeing or captured by thieves—he should recite this.
"Having extracted the *viśvavatī* verse that removes disease, one should employ the others;
Śaunaka maintains that one should recite this entire hymn," so it is said.
Restrained for three nights and fasting, he should cook a sacrificial porridge of milk-rice;
with that, the twice-born man should offer a full hundred oblations of clarified butter.
Having dedicated [the offering] to the Great God Tryambaka with the verse beginning "Tryambaka," and having performed this hundred-fold rite,
one shall live happily for a hundred years.
One who desires to live a long life should worship the Sun after bathing with the verse beginning "That eye" (RgV 7.66.16), while he is rising and when he has reached the meridian.

Rigveda 2.27 (145a): He who, having risen at the latter part of the night, being self-controlled and pure; Rigveda 2.28 (145b): Should worship with the six hymns beginning with "vyuṣā," with palms joined in reverence.
He shall obtain abundant wealth in various forms, such as gold and the like;
cows, horses, men, grain, women, garments, goats, and sheep.
While reciting this [hymn] while bound in these fixed dwellings, one is released;
standing at night, one should recite it, and thus one attains freedom from the fetters.
Remaining thus for day and night, fasting and motionless,
his iron fetters burst asunder, and likewise his wooden bonds.

Restrained and constant, one should always take refuge in the goddess Earth with the words, "O pleasant one. One should also recite this [verse] there; thus, one is released from the bond of the earth.
Whatever sin one may commit through action, thought, or speech—
by muttering this verse beginning with "yat kiṃ ca idam varuṇa," one is liberated from it.
This expiation is prescribed for approaching a woman who should not be approached;
except in the case of violating the teacher’s bed, one is thereby released from that sin.
One who has approached a woman of his own lineage should recite [the Veda] while fasting for twelve days;
one who has lived with the wife of a friend should do so while fasting for half a month.
"O Waters, carry away this, whatever impurity is here, and this verse again"—
with these words, one should enter the water and mutter them during these rites.
Having paid homage to Indra and Viṣṇu, one who desires his own prosperity should offer clarified butter daily with these two hymns that follow.
Having waded into the water up to his mouth, facing the east, self-restrained and pure,
he should worship the sun with these two hymns, three times each.
One who desires rain should diligently recite this while fasting;
when five nights have passed, one shall obtain a great downpour.
He who might be assailed by enemies or falsely accused,
having fasted for one three-night period, should offer clarified butter daily.
One should recite this hymn beginning with "indrāsomā" at least one hundred times;
at the conclusion, one should give something to the twice-born, and thus one overcomes all enemies.

If a twice-born man’s vow should be violated through delusion, or if he should come into contact with Vrātyas, he should fast and offer clarified butter with the mantra: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows."
Reciting "pra saṃrājam," one should gaze at the sun;
having bathed day after day, one should worship it as it rises.
But he who is assailed or even disputes with anyone,
having conquered his enemies along with their hosts, shall quickly win the debate.
One should enter [the ritual] with the mantra "śam agnir agnibhiś ca"; having praised Vāyu and Bhāskara, and having first praised Agni, one is released from great distress.
Indeed, he who, having risen early in the morning and bathed, worships with the four verses beginning with "na hi," protects himself from fear for two months.
Having recited this triplet beginning with "āyat," and having bathed and worshipped Indra (Puraṃdara),
one shall obtain all mental desires by fully honoring the radiant Vasus.
The first three hymns, as well as the five beginning with "bṛhan," and likewise the final six hymns, including "agnim naro" and "itaḥ," [are to be recited].
One should recite this chapter, "The Primary Subjects" (Prakṛtāni), prior to a meal;
by doing so, one attains all desires and is liberated from all sins.

This sacred prayer (*brahman*) is for the great seers (*maharṣi*) among men; for one who recites it constantly in the forenoon before eating, the supreme accomplishment of their purpose shall come to pass.
The hymn beginning with "agninā" is the twenty-four-verse hymn dedicated to the Aśvins;
one should recite it daily at dawn, having become pure and being observant of good vows, after having worshipped the two Nāsatyas.
He shall attain supreme prosperity, as well as wealth and vigor,
who offers clarified butter into the fire with each verse of this hymn, saying "With fuel" (samidhā).
Having attained incomparable perfection, he lives for a hundred years equal [to others] by means of this hymn of forty-two verses, "agha," addressed here to the wielder of the thunderbolt.

Having obtained friendship with the great Indra, he lays low many rivals. One should consume [the food] while muttering [the mantra] here; having posed the question, one should act according to the authoritative rule.
Therefore, this morning recitation is remembered as the destroyer of enemies;
by chanting the hymn beginning with "vāśam mahī," one likewise attains perfect health.
Having recited the *duhsvapnaghnī* hymns in the morning, one is liberated from sins;
likewise, having eaten food while self-controlled and pure, one should recite the two verses beginning with *śam no bhava*.
Having touched his heart with his hand, may he live long, free from disease and happy. From whichever direction one perceives danger, there one should remain restrained in one's vows.
Having established the fire in a pure place and having worshipped Indra, one should offer oblations;
having purified the clarified butter with the mantra beginning "yataḥ" and having presented the six fragrances.
One should offer milk-rice, curd-mash, or even cakes;
having fasted for one day and night, one should likewise offer sesame seeds or clarified butter.
Having bathed and offered oblations with the hymn beginning "ut tvā mandantu," one should cause one's enemies to perish;
whether bound or unbound, one should recite it with speech controlled and mind composed.
By reciting the hymn beginning with *tyān nu* (Ṛgveda 1.106), which has the Ādityas as its deity, one is immediately released from bondage.
One who is self-restrained and pure should constantly mutter the *pragātha* verse beginning with *yad dyāvā* (Ṛgveda 1.159).
Having attained incomparable fame, he enjoys all his desires;
having offered oblations with the hymn beginning "tvam no agne" (RgV 1.187) and having worshipped Agni with clarified butter.
Protected on all sides by his radiance, he shall obtain wealth through the Fire;
indeed, by means of this hymn, he shall constantly attain riches as great as those of Indra.
To him whose hand has been pacified, the slayer of Vṛtra bestows wealth.
One who is self-restrained should constantly recite the hymn beginning with "kanyā vāraḥ."
One should quickly free from that [condition] a woman who suffers from skin diseases or is hairless,
after praising Purandara with the hymn "yad adya kac ca" when the sun has risen.
Chanting, he drives away impurity or brings the world under his control;
whoever, being firm in his vows, approaches with these two verses beginning with "Speech" (vāk) and worships Gaurī.
No unrefined speech ever issues from his mouth.
Having seen the sun, he should stand before it reciting the two verses beginning with "baṇ mahām.
Even while speaking an untruthful word, he is not defiled by falsehood.
One should cultivate the thought: "This is the moonlight of the full moon."
One who has seen the moon becomes unblinking, radiant, and possessed of keen vision;
by bathing and muttering "Prajā ha," one is not born again from a womb.
By touching a cow and reciting "The Mother," one obtains cattle;
but by reciting "The Knower of Speech" over this [cow], one obtains speech.
One should recite this ninth maṇḍala, the Pāvamāna, which is supreme.
Having bathed, being pure in a clean place, wearing a purifier (pavitra) and accompanied by gold. A twice-born man should recite the Gāyatrī verses of the Pāvamāna beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā."
One should mutter the Pāvamānī verses, for they are the purification among purifications.
RgV_3.1.(2a): One who, being self-restrained, immerses oneself in water, is quickly liberated from all sins.
RgV_3.1.(2b): Likewise, the recitation, the remembrance, and the retention of these [verses] are meritorious.
Having understood these according to their true nature, one attains the world of Brahman;
for among those qualities as they have been described, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
By reciting it, one becomes purified; by remembering it, one remembers the Supreme. By retaining it in memory, one whose self is purified and whose senses are conquered attains the state of Brahman.
Having understood it according to its true nature, one attains the state of Brahman.
One should cause the deities to hear [the recitation] while the Brāhmaṇas are eating in front.
RgV 3.2.6ab: That [offering] pleases the deity and brings that ritual action to fulfillment.
RgV 3.2.6cd: In the rite for the ancestors, the ancestors are pleased when they are summoned by one whose self is restrained.
Having committed even very great offenses, such as drinking what should not be drunk and so forth,
and having swallowed [such things], one becomes pure after three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn and entering into water.
And that which is given to the ancestors shall become inexhaustible, a supreme honey,
for one who studies the *pāvamānī* verses with a purified self and conquered senses.
To him, cows become wish-fulfilling milch-cows;
they attend upon him with long life, strength, glory, wealth, progeny, fame, and health.
One who is purified attains incomparable and imperishable merit through the study of the Veda;
however, one who is unable [to perform rituals] should recite the *pavitra* mantras and those that follow them with focused devotion.
Those which were proclaimed by the seven seers, and those which are the supreme [verses] of the Pavitra;
this collection of sixty-two *ṛc*s beginning with "pavasva" was proclaimed by the most excellent of seers.
For the destruction of all impurities, for purification, and for auspiciousness,
sixty-seven hymns beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā" are proclaimed here.
RgV 3.3.13a: There are ten hundred [verses], namely one thousand, of the *pāvamānī* verses of the Ṛgveda.
RgV 3.3.13b: By offering these in sacrifice and reciting them, one shall conquer even the terrible fear of death.
One obtains liberation from diseases; there is no doubt about this.
[This applies even] after accepting what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured.
By reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn while entering the waters, one becomes pure after three days;
for this *Pāvamāna* hymn is the supreme remover of sins.
Having restrained the vital breaths, one should meditate at the conclusion upon the gods, the ancestors, and the seers;
having fasted, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and worship Agni and Soma.
One should worship Sarasvatī with milk, water, honey, and clarified butter;
having recited that purifying hymn concerning the inner self, one becomes bathed and pure.
One attains the desired goal and finds prosperity in this world.
Having fasted, one should mutter the *Pāvamāna* hymns a hundred thousand times;
according to the word of Vasiṣṭha, this indeed destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
At the time of death, one should recite once the hymns beginning with "nānānam."
Having recited it, one attains the supreme station and immortality.
A twice-born man, being self-restrained, should always employ the hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha."
One who desires purity for the sake of bathing should recite [the hymn] three times with a concentrated mind;
having immersed oneself in the waters, one should likewise recite it three times with great composure.
But the killer of a Brahmin shall wander for twelve years with a skull [as a begging bowl], carrying a staff topped by a skull, and clothed in rags, proclaiming his own deed.
One should recite this mentally, remembering "āpo hi ṣṭha" (Rig Veda 10.9.1);
however, after the fifth year, one should indeed recite it a thousand times aloud.
Furthermore, there should always be a recitation of three thousand [verses] every day;
when the twelfth year is complete, even a slayer of a Brahmin is fully liberated.
Having assembled, the Brahmins should speak to him who has completed his vow: "Has anything been left unperformed? Or has the Lord been addressed with falsehood?"
RgV_3.5.(25a): You shall slay ten descendants and ten ancestors by speaking untruth.
RgV_3.5.(25b): Having been permitted by the learned brahmins, one who is pure should say "Om, bhoḥ" and then recite [the mantra].
And he should prepare a meal cooked in a pot for the one who maintains the vow by the sacred fire;
thus, having undertaken the Sāvitrī, he is released from evil.
O Śakra, in former times, having slain the illustrious Ṛṣi, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, you were a slayer of a Brahmin;
Sindhudvīpa, by means of these [verses], consecrated you and released you from that [guilt].
Having committed the theft of a Brahmin’s property or the wealth of a guru, one is liberated from that sin after six years by reciting these [verses] according to this very procedure.
Even a slayer of a Brahmin or a drinker of liquor, by reciting these with discipline,
is released from sin through this very practice, just like a killer of a Brahmin.
Having raised his hand against a Brahmin in anger, one should mutter these [verses];
having struck him down, one should fast for three days; and having merely threatened him, one should fast for one day.
But having somehow caused blood to flow by a blow,
one should fast for exactly three nights and recite these [verses] after propitiating him.
Rising early in the morning, one should constantly perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) for oneself;
it is the atonement for sins committed during the night that were previously unrecognized.
And every evening, one should perform the ritual purification of oneself with these [verses];
it is the atonement for sins committed during the day that were not consciously recognized.
A twice-born man should worship King Yama with the hymn [beginning with] "yam" (RgV 10.14),
and he should prepare a dish of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) dedicated to Yama on both fortnights.
On the eighth and the fourteenth [lunar days], one should sacrifice to Yama with an oblation;
for this occasion, one should employ the hymn beginning with "pareyivāṃsam."
Before the end of his lifespan, he shall never die by any means whatsoever;
King Yama is pleased with him and grants him recollection at the final moment.

At the end of the mantra, one should offer the oblation with the words, "Svāhā to the King of Dharma. On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform this rite as a regular obligation.
He who, having bathed on the new moon or on festival days, offers water with sesame seeds to Yama and his retinue, does not encounter any fear.
O Death, by reciting this [hymn] for a full year, eating only at night and restricting his food, the twice-born man shall indeed attain the Supreme Death.
Death shall not lead him away before his full span of life, along with his sons and progeny. By subsisting on fruits and eating sparingly, one may conquer death within three years.
At the sixth mealtime, however, he should eat fruit or even roots;
he should pass his time through alternating standing and sitting, and he should dwell in the water during the cold season.
In the summer he should practice the five-fire penance, while in the rainy season he should dwell under the open sky;
thus disciplined, he shall conquer death and be liberated from diseases.

When the husband has died childless, the brother-in-law, desiring to ascend [the funeral pyre] for the sake of progeny with his brother’s wife who is intent on doing so, should turn her back with the words, "Arise! (RgV 3.8.43ab).
When the fertile period has arrived, anointed with clarified butter and restrained in speech,
he should procreate one son, and by no means a second.
One should recollect the ten-syllable mantra "Bhadraṃ naḥ" for the sake of peace;
having become pure, one should chant it constantly and attains mental happiness.
For one month he should subsist on fruits, and for another month he should drink only water;
then, for one month, he should subsist on air while reciting this [hymn] thousands of times.
By the mind alone, all his desired objects are accomplished;
he beholds the divine Gandharvas, and he beholds the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
He becomes invisible from this world and moves through the sky;
like Parameṣṭhin, he sees from afar and hears from afar.
One who is disciplined should recite "pra devatrā" in the desert lands of the Maruts;
when a danger as fatal as death has arrived, he quickly finds water.
One should perfume three dice made of vibhītaka wood with fragrant substances;
having placed them in the air, one should scatter flowers over them.
Having joined his feet together, he should stand through that night reciting the hymn to Akṣa;
however, this verse beginning with "prāvepā mā" he should recite in his mind alone during the night.
When the night has dawned and the sun has risen, one should go to the assembly of the gods while reciting this [hymn].
One should always recite this very hymn; thus one conquers others and is not conquered by them.
Whomever one may wish to conquer, one should touch him on the head and recite this hymn;
by the remainder of the hymn, one conquers others and is not conquered by anyone.
One should recite "abudhram uṣāsā naktā" (Rigveda 3.10.54a) for the sake of a safe journey;
and one should constantly recite "namo mitrasya varuṇasya cakṣase" (Rigveda 3.10.54b).
And there is one final verse of this very hymn by which one is released from sins;
with that one should constantly offer clarified butter, and thus one is completely liberated from sins.
One endowed with faith should mutter the hymn beginning with "divas pari" (Rg Veda 3.11).
One who desires faith, being composed in mind, obtains faith everywhere.
One who mutters "May we not go astray" on a path through the thicket is a fool;
yet, he proceeds safely along the way and finds supreme bliss.
If one should think of any dear friend that their life has come to an end, one who has bathed should touch the head of that person while reciting, "Thine is Yama. (Rigveda 3.11.58ab)
If one recites this five times a thousand times for five days, one shall obtain long life;
one should anoint him with the *sūkta* of Ghṛta using the [text] of Sindhudvīpa.
While constantly reclining upon his bed, he should indeed mutter this mantra;
thereafter, he may touch his sons, his wife, other loved ones, and himself.
One should constantly employ this *jīvā-vṛtti* with clarified butter;
by anointing all the sense organs with it, one becomes happy and free from feverish affliction.
This mantra, "idam itthā," is said to be a yielder of a thousandfold reward. For half a month one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya), and for half a month one should drink milk.
Having fasted during the latter fortnight, staying in the forest upon a pure, cleared space,
and having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, one should offer clarified butter into the flame.
The *sruk*, the *sruva*, and the *camasa*—all these should be made of *udumbara* wood. By offering a thousand oblations with them, one is united with whatever desire one has.
One should know that this ritual action is indeed not in vain, for it certainly brings about success;
even if it is partially futile, it still yields half of its fruit.
One desiring food should offer clarified butter at a crossroads while facing the sun;
one desiring wealth, however, should feed a thousand twice-born men.
One desiring cattle should mutter [this hymn] in a cow-pen, or, having fasted, one should offer oblations;
by this rule, being self-restrained, one obtains a thousand cattle.
One should have a three-stranded amulet made of copper, red stone, and gold;
and there should be a thousand fuel-sticks over which oblations have been poured with the *sampāta* formula.
Having performed the *sahasrasampāta* oblation, one should indeed carry it on one's head;
or, having become pure, one may hold it with the hand, and thus one becomes a follower of the Thousandfold Path.
The hymn *Parāvataḥ* is prescribed as a means for securing well-being for a *snātaka*. One who desires heaven should constantly recite it, remaining firm in his vows.
One should constantly recite the hymn of praise for knowledge beginning with "O Bṛhaspati, first...
(RgV 3.14). One becomes possessed of knowledge, becomes glorious, and attains infinite prosperity.
For the purpose of destroying misfortune, the twice-born should subsist on milk;
by reciting this verse, "vayaḥ suparṇā," he indeed attains prosperity.
But he who, enveloped by darkness, might think of himself as the Self within the self,
or even if possessed by misfortune, is liberated by muttering this [hymn].
Having risen in the morning, one should always rub one's eyes with this [verse];
thus one becomes possessed of sight, endowed with splendor, and drives away misfortune.
Reciting this verse, "Na taṃ vidātha," with a concentrated mind, the wise man,
having cast off all impurity, attains the eternal Brahman.
Whoever, having bathed on the festival days (parvan), should offer water with sesame seeds to Yama together with his retinue,
finds no fear from that.
One should always mutter these two [hymns] beginning with "O Manyu, you who slay rivals" (RgV 3.14) while offering oblations of clarified butter; with these two, one should wear an iron amulet.
One should offer an iron stake with these two verses on the fourteenth day;
when the fire is kindled with fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood, it repels one's rivals.
Just as the supreme Brahman is secret, purifying, and wonderful, so too is this heart-pleasing charm; indeed, nothing superior to it exists.
Having fasted for twelve days, constantly reciting this Ṛṣi,
one should remain focused on it with self-restraint, approaching the waters three times a day.
At the end of the twelve-day rite, being composed in a pure place,
he should likewise fashion an image of a man out of earth upon the ground.
Having stepped upon her heart region, one should mutter the Ṛṣi-mantra;
one should know that the rite is unfailing once a day and night have passed.
In three days one may recover from a Vaiśya who is wealthy; in four nights, from a Kṣatriya;
in five nights, from a king; and in six nights, from the highest of the twice-born.
One may overcome an ascetic after seven nights and then eat him;
or else, having fasted and bathed, one should constantly remain intent on reciting this.
He who desires to make himself inferior should avoid [the following]:
one should cause the powder of *bilva* fruits to be sprinkled over an oblation offered with a thousand [drops] falling together.
Just as one leads a beast to a watering hole, he should quickly bring that person under his control—
whether it be toward their mother, themselves, their sons, father, brothers, or friends.
One should apply this which is dear to the heart and bear the teacher upon one's head; but having embraced a good friend and smelled the crown of his head, one should likewise honor one's own son.
One should employ this [hymn], which is heart-pleasing, for the sake of pacification and for happiness;
when a reconciliation has not been achieved, one should fashion an image out of dust on the path.
If a Brāhmaṇa, having kindled the fire, should offer oblations with clarified butter;
but for a Kṣatriya, with oil, and for the Vaiśyas as well, with mustard-seed oil.
Or one should have an iron image placed in the midst of the fire;
and perceiving it as ablaze, one should offer oblations with a focused mind and purified self.
With a fierce mind one should strike, and being enraged, one should offer clarified butter;
in whatever manner it is offered into the blazing Jātavedas.
A Brahmin whose appearance is radiant shall likewise come under his control.
One should construct a distinctive altar from the ashes of those burned in a cremation ground.
When a fire is kindled with fuel-sticks of the *vaibhītaka* tree, one should place an image made of iron [into it]. At midnight, while standing in sesame oil mixed with mustard seeds and salt.
In that rite, one should prepare a sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) made of *śara* reeds in a reverse order;
