then, sitting upon three stakes, the one of fierce appearance should offer oblations.
With disheveled hair and seeking slaughter, one would achieve success before long;
or else, practicing *abhicāra* (malevolent magic), one should thus offer one's own blood as an oblation.
It brings the king under control, as well as the people and the city, quickly. Furthermore, the rite for prosperity should be performed with a pleasing [hymn] by one who has self-restraint.
A Brahmin should not commit an act involving the killing of one who is innocent;
he should prepare a sacrificial pap (caru) with the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same color.
One should cause the first-born calf to drink [the milk] offered with a thousand oblations;
that calf shall have a thousand followers and be free from passions.
One should also cause the cows to drink [the water], and they become free from fever;
one should always feed one's sons, as well as other dear ones and virtuous people.
They become free from disease, gracious, and devoid of fever. If one should desire a woman, this is a great means of winning her favor.
One skilled in the ritual should heat with fire the fine powder of rice grains split by the fingernails, which have been offered in a thousand oblations.
One should fashion an image of her; having meditated upon that woman with the mind, one should offer oblations limb by limb, anointed with mustard oil.
One should first cut off the two feet and cause them to be placed in the fire with the utterance "phaṭ.
Then [one should cut off] the shanks, the knees, the thighs, the arms, and thereafter the head.
Having cut the region of the heart, one should fix it within one's own heart;
by reciting this [mantra], the wise man brings that woman under his control.
O best of the twice-born, one should never perform [this rite] with women who are protected by others, nor with those who are virtuous,
nor with those devoted to dharma, vows, and good conduct.
If a man should have intercourse with women of lower caste who have been taken by him through lust, he would make her husband virtuous; yet, she herself remains as she was before.

Having eaten milk-rice and immediately vomited it up, one should have it set aside. That powder should be given to the wife of a dark-complexioned man; this is known as a means of winning her affection (*saṃvanana*).
In this manner, one should consecrate an odd number of fruits from a large tree with mantras;
of these, one should eat the even-numbered ones oneself and leave the remaining half.
One who recites this Ṛṣi-mantra should offer those [oblations] if he wishes to bring someone under his control.
It is taught that this rite of conciliation (*saṃvanana*) should be performed by one who, having become a friend, seeks to win over an enemy.

However, one should [recite] each single verse that is suitable and pleasing, beginning with a *sūkta*; furthermore, one who acts according to his desire should perform the ritual actions in a manner that is fitting.
The wise know that this rite for the slave Parāka, spoken from the heart, is a means of winning over women;
it is also prescribed for men.
One should always recite [the mantra] against those who are hateful among one's own kinsmen during battle. One should have a stake made of *khadira* wood and drive it into the heart [of the enemy].
Having first fashioned an effigy out of dust or even from husks,
and having consecrated even an arrow with mantras, one should engage in battle.
One should know this [hymn] as the "Slayer of Foes," employed for invincibility; it is remembered as a heart-pleasing charm for the purpose of overcoming enemies, slaves, and those who hate.
Even by contemplating these two hymns with the mind, one attains success. Furthermore, the father should cause the maiden to hear the *bhāvavṛtta* regarding Sūryā.
"By this [verse], a maiden shall find a husband who is suitable and well-matched to her;
she should constantly mutter 'imām' while touching her navel. (RgV 3.22.116ab)
The husband should likewise recite this; then they both shall be long-lived. And the brother, or even the father, should bathe the maiden with suitable [verses].
"May she have ten sons and never be separated from her husband;
may she be a sovereign queen"—reciting this, one should constantly touch the head of the maiden.
She is honored by her mother-in-law, father-in-law, brother-in-law, and sisters-in-law;
one should employ this hymn for bathing, which records the dialogue with Indrāṇī.
This hymn, consisting of nine sections and joined by the final [verse], bestows a husband’s good fortune and sons;
it is filled with heaps of water-born flowers and surrounded by variegated jars.
In this matter, a sacrifice must likewise be performed for Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
and also for Bhaga, for the Apsarases, and for the Lord of the Yakṣas.
For Indrāṇī, the wife of the gods, as well as for Rati and Pradyumna,
[one should perform the rite] with vessels filled with river water and *salila*, and surrounded by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having offered oblations into the fire, one should bathe the maiden while she stands in the southern region;
her hair should be rubbed with a decoction of *priyaṅgu*, *vaṭa*, and *nāga* trees.
Having performed the *sampāta* oblation accompanied by all medicinal herbs, one should indeed consecrate them at the end of the hymn with the nine verses beginning with "vi hi. (RgV 3.24).
One should sprinkle her who has fasted with water drawn from a vessel full of stable water;
for by this very means, those bodies of women who are hostile toward their husbands are indeed pacified.
One should bathe [the victim] with the *āhanasyā* verses, knowing that which is called *vipravrājinī*.
One should extract this from the hymn (*sūkta*), but not the two-verse section beginning with "na seśe."
This [hymn] has been taught by some for the performance of human action;
one should mutter this "rakṣohaṇam vājinam" [verse], which is a slayer of demons.
Having kindled the fire, one should constantly worship it with this [hymn];
and one should offer oblations of clarified butter with it; thereby one repels the *rakṣas* demons.
This is the slayer of demons; it is proclaimed as the supreme peace.
One should employ this hymn, known as the *Haviṣpāntīya*, on this occasion.
In the event of partaking of food that is censured or associated with sin, one should practice the *Haviṣpāntīya* hymn;
for this is the supreme purifier and should be meditated upon constantly.
Having fixed his gaze upon the sun, disciplined and self-controlled, he should practice for six months;
he then beholds the path of the gods within the solar orb.
The Vaiśvānara-vidyā belonging to him shines forth, established within his own body;
by practicing the Haviṣpāntīya [hymn], he is liberated from all sins.
One should mutter the hymn beginning with "I praise Indra," which destroys enemies;
it is the purifier among purifiers, a secret, wondrous means of purification.
In the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation and in a good pasture,
one who desires a son should, on the twelfth lunar day, prepare a sacrificial pap (caru) dedicated to Viṣṇu.
On the eleventh day, the husband and wife should observe a fast at a beautiful temple;
having properly worshipped Janārdana with the sixteen *ṛc* verses.
One desiring a son should cook a sacrificial oblation (caru) while reciting the Puruṣasūkta;
he shall soon obtain a son devoted to Viṣṇu, capable of perpetuating the lineage.
One should properly offer twelve oblations of twelve-fold portions, prepared with milk as a sacrificial pap (*caru*).
He who performs this shall possess a thousand [attendants] and go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having offered oblations into the fire properly and according to rule with the sixteen Ṛgvedic verses, the wise man,
with palms joined in reverence, should perform a hymn of praise using those same verses.
One should remember Keśava in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and Nārāyaṇa is remembered in Pauṣa;
one should remember Mādhava in the month of Māgha, and likewise Govinda in Phālguna.
In Caitra one should know Viṣṇu, and likewise Madhusūdana in Vaiśākha;
in Jyeṣṭha one should know Trivikrama, and they know Vāmana in Āṣāḍha.
One should know Śrīdhara in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and Hṛṣīkeśa thereafter; Padmanābha in Āśvina, and Dāmodara in Kārttika.
The sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga has declared these twelve names;
by honoring [the months] with their names, one attains all desires.
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence;
likewise, one who is wealthy, possessed of progeny, righteous, and virtuous.
Having offered fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree into the fire, one should offer oblations again;
having meditated upon the worship of the consumer of oblations and honored the Slayer of Madhu.
Thereafter, being pure and restraining his speech, he should perform the oblation of the *havis* verse by verse;
he should offer clarified butter with a *sūkta*, as was done previously at the beginning and the end.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa as her husband,
and having consumed the remainder of the sacrificial oblation, the woman, having received the blessing, should go to bed for the night.
Then, having performed this rite, the satiation of the twice-born (brahmins) must be carried out. He should abstain from a second wife until she conceives a child.
Whether she be childless, or whose children have died, or she who gives birth only to daughters—
may she quickly give birth to a son, just as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga declared.
I shall fully proclaim the hymn of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable,
by performing which all sages attain the Brahman-nirvāṇa.
In water, in fire, in the heart, in the sun, on the sacrificial ground,
and in images— in these six places, the sages have declared that the worship of Hari is performed correctly.
The God [Hari] is in the fire for those who perform ritual actions; He is the God in heaven for the wise;
He is in idols for those of limited intellect; and He is in the hearts of yogis.

For water is his abode; therefore Hari is always present within them. And because he is omnipresent, he is likewise present upon the sacrificial ground for those who have cultivated their inner selves.
Whoever should offer flowers or even water with the Puruṣasūkta,
by him this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, would be worshipped.
The deity of this hymn, which is composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter and concludes with a *triṣṭubh*, is the Puruṣa who is the seed of the universe; he is remembered as the seer Nārāyaṇa.
O Nārāyaṇa of mighty arms, O Lord, listen with a one-pointed mind;
I shall explain to you the ritual procedure for the recitation of the Puruṣasūkta in relation to worship.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, facing east with a purified mind, one should perform the fire-rite, the recitation procedure, and the hymn consisting of the six-fold self.
One should place the first [syllable] on the left hand, the second on the right hand;
one should place the third on the left foot and the fourth on the right.
One should place the fifth [syllable] on the left knee and the sixth on the right;
the seventh on the left hip and the eighth on the right hip.
One should place the ninth [syllable] in the middle of the navel, the tenth in the heart;
the eleventh in the region of the throat, and the twelfth on the left arm.
One should place the thirteenth [syllable] on the right face and the fourteenth on the left;
one should place the fifteenth on the two eyes and the sixteenth on the head.

Having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should thereafter commence the worship; having performed the ritual placement according to the rules upon the deity just as one has done upon one's own body.
With the first verse, one should invoke the Supreme Puruṣa;
with the second, one should offer a seat; and with the third, water for the feet.
The water for honoring (arghya) should be given with the fourth [case ending], and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) with the fifth;
one should perform the bath with the sixth, and likewise the garment with the seventh.
On the eighth day, the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) [should be offered], and on the ninth, ointment;
on the tenth, flowers should be given, and on the eleventh, incense.
On the twelfth day, one should offer the lamp; on the thirteenth, the food offering;
on the fourteenth, the prostration; and on the fifteenth, the circumambulation.

One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) during the bathing, the clothing, and the food offering (naivedya). Furthermore, one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given according to one's ability, specifically with the sixteenth verse.

Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) with a concentrated mind. Having recited the hymn (*sūkta*) according to one's ability, one should then offer it to him.
On the right side of the deity, one should have a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) prepared using the first [mantra];
with the second, however, one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
With the third [verse], one should place the fire; with the fourth, the kindling;
with the fifth, the cooking of the clarified butter and likewise the cooking of the sacrificial oblation.
With the sixth [syllable], one should indeed fashion a lotus seat in the midst of the fire;
one should meditate upon the Lord of the God of Gods, whose splendor is equal to the fire of time (Kālānala).
Then, having requested permission, one should offer fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, starting from the seventh day and proceeding in due order.

First, one should offer as many clarified butter-drenched fuel-sticks (*samidh*) as there are; then one should offer with ghee, and thereafter again with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). Having offered in this manner, one should then request permission in the proper sequence.
RgV_3.32.(173b): One should recite a hymn of praise in the presence of that blessed Agni.
RgV_3.33.(174a): Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
RgV_3.33.(174b): Let there be salutation to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Being, O Primordial One!
O Lord, who is common to both the gods and the dānavas as their presiding deity,
I always go for refuge to you, whose two feet are my refuge.
You alone are the creator of the world and likewise its destroyer;
you are the unmanifest and the witness, veiled by the power of the guṇas and māyā.
Having obtained you alone as their refuge, the wise cross over the terrible, endless ocean of saṃsāra, which is a vessel of afflictions.
Neither your form, nor your appearance, nor your weapons, nor your abode can be perceived;
nevertheless, you manifest in the form of a person to your devotees.
Nothing at all is hidden from you; you are not hidden from anyone. Nothing at all is unattainable for you; nor are you to be attained by anyone.
They know Your station to be the primordial cause of all effects, the highest of all words,
and the supreme perfection of the yogis.
O Lord of Gods, I am afraid in this great terror of saṃsāra.
O lotus-eyed one, protect me; I do not know the supreme state.
O Acyuta, at all times and in all directions, you have entered my body; great fear dwells within me.
Other than Your lotus feet, there is nothing else for me, even in future births—
having attained this realization and having secured this station.
O God, may there never be a depletion of this [merit] for me even in another birth;
even if I am born into a miserable state, may my heart’s desire remain fixed upon you.
If I do not meet with destruction, I shall always be content with that much alone;
I desire only the feet of Viṣṇu in all my births.
This hymn to Puruṣa Hari brings about heaven, wealth, and fame;
it is this merit-bestowing knowledge of the Self, this supreme knowledge of Yoga.
Subsisting on fruit for a month, he beholds the Self within the self;
having eaten fruits, he should fast for a month and subsist only on water.
One should dwell constantly in the forest, always reciting this seer’s hymn; with a concentrated mind, one should bathe in the waters three times during the three periods of the day.
One should constantly worship the Āditya with this hymn;
having offered oblations of clarified butter with this very hymn, one should meditate upon this seer.
Subsisting on fruits for one month, he shall conquer heaven within three years;
devoted to that, focused on that, and disciplined, he who has no other object of devotion shall do so within ten years.
He beholds face to face that god Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment;
the imperishable creator of the world, who is to be grasped only with the utmost effort.
One should abide by the duties of a householder, established in justice and pure in one's vows;
one should meditate upon this god, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction.
At midnight, having abandoned sleep and arisen, pure in speech and self-restrained,
the knower of yoga should practice yoga while all beings are fast asleep.
Sitting upright on level ground, in a place free from wind and devoid of noise,
one should then place the left foot upon the right knee.
Having drawn back his right foot and placing it upon his left knee,
he remains composed with palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, his eyes closed in meditative absorption.
Having uttered "Om," one should contemplate one's own heart without hesitation;
there, one should compose the self, as well as the senses and the mind.
When he does not perceive anything else, nor see, nor hear,
nor even reflect in his mind— that state is called the attainment of yoga.
One should practice this beloved Ṛṣi as if seeing him before one's eyes according to the sacred revelation;
having restrained the vital breaths while seated, one should contemplate that Ṛṣi for as long as it takes.
Having brought the mind down below the navel as if about to exhale, one should exhale in this manner repeatedly; with the mind fixed on that, one should advance in yoga.
For one who thus applies [the mind] in this way, one would neither see nor hear common objects;
then, one should gradually lead the mind upward from the heart.
The two clavicles, the mouth, the nose, the eyes, and the eyebrows are equal [in their placement]. Between the eyebrows is the supreme station; there one should fix this [mind] steadily.
Then, having held it at the region of the forehead, one should lead it to the head;
exhaling at the proper time, and having reached the navel, one should exhale again.
This is declared to be the supreme station of Brahman, the Supreme Self. One who is thus disciplined attains the Great Self, which is one's own self.
Whether one be a doer of good deeds and pure, or even the worst of evildoers,
upon perceiving the Supreme Brahman and knowing the Goal, one becomes purified.
If one is bound by all sins, having understood this, one should recite it with self-restraint;
even from mere desire to know it, one shall go to the supreme goal.
This concentration (dhāraṇā) must be performed separately and constantly according to this rule:
one should fix [the mind] upon the sun, the fire, the moon, and the tops of trees.
Whether on a mountain peak, by the ocean, or wherever the mind finds delight,
one should never, under any circumstances, maintain the senses once they have encountered their objects.
One should know that there is much suffering here when concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is performed [but not perfected] at the time of death;
however, one who has fallen from yoga is reborn into a pure family of the righteous.
When one finds that Brahman at the crown of the head, that very best of seers,
then one should lead that supreme light from the crown upward along the path of the stars.
Having attained mastery over yoga, the yogi, free from dualities and knowing the supreme Self,
should everywhere behold the Self by means of the self, being devoted to the Seer.
And having bathed, one should always recite this supreme purifier;
even one joined with great sins shall, in time, become a doer of good deeds.
Constantly devoted to austerity, truthful in speech, and free from malice,
the wise sage who recites this Ṛṣi shall in due time become a possessor of wealth.
With whatever desire one should constantly recite this Ṛṣi,
that very desire shall be fulfilled for the person who acts with faith.
Whether it be a fire-oblation, or a muttered prayer, or an offering, or a sacrificial pap—
one should perform that by which one may ascertain the fulfillment of whatever desire one has.
Supremacy among kinsmen, great wealth, fame, the highest state in this world,
and liberation from evil— one should understand that these constitute its success.
Having reached the eternal Brahman— which is attainable through knowledge, supremely subtle, all-pervading, and established as the substrate of all— one should grasp it with the utmost effort.
The hymn beginning with "sahasra-śīrṣā" bestows the fruit of all desires;
indeed, he who possesses a body that is the womb of the Vedas is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
In this hymn, Brahmā, Indu, Rudra, and Parjanya are established;
this entire world, both stationary and moving, is to be seen as residing herein.
Even if we do not attain devotion, one should not neglect it;
for the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is heard to be compassionate toward his devotees.

For the sake of worshipping that deity, one should daily offer an oblation of wild grains gathered by oneself, according to the rules for forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka-vidhāna*), by pouring the sacrificial food (*caru*) while reciting at the end of the mantra: "Svāhā to Nārāyaṇa! (RgV 3.41).
From that [offering], he bestows upon the Hotṛ priest divine vision extending to a thousand [yojanas].
Or else, one may offer a thousand carus by means of a single ritual procedure (tantra).
Or as many as can be completed in a single day, he should finish them all;
he obtains the fruit of a thousand desired objects and wishes.

Endowed with a lifespan equal to that of a man, or even as a perfected being (siddha), one may wander the earth. Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the center of the orb of the sun, seated upon a lotus throne, should be meditated upon constantly—
wearing armlets, makara-shaped earrings, a crown, and a necklace, possessing a golden body, and bearing the conch and the discus.
But he who merely recites this hymn, having paid homage to the venerable feet of Nārāyaṇa,
goes by that supreme recitation to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu, which is free from old age and death.
The wise constantly worship Hari in the fire with oblations, in the water with flowers, in the heart through meditation,
and in the solar orb through the recitation of prayers.
The leaf of the *bilva*, the leaf of the *śamī*, and the leaf of the *bhṛṅgarāja*,
as well as the *mālatī*, *kuśa*, and *padma*— these bring immediate satisfaction to Hari.
Whatever is not attainable, one should meditate upon that with the mind alone;
through the grace of the God of gods, the wielder of the discus, it is indeed accomplished.
With leaves, flowers, and water—always obtained without purchase—one should always offer these to the virtuous.
Why, then, is no effort made for the sake of liberation toward that Ancient Person who is attainable through devotion alone?

Thus has been declared the procedure for the worship of the Puruṣa Viṣṇu by the one named Viṣṇukumāra; however, having observed that the injunctions spoken here by Nārada serve to awaken [beings] to the single path of liberation, [this other method is set forth].

One who is constant in his vows should daily recite those *oṣadhi* hymns that bring well-being; he should also constantly win over the plants for six months without fail. Having performed a sacrifice to Rudra in the autumn, one should likewise worship the plants.
For him there are no diseases, nor those which have already become chronic.
One should perform this ritual for seven nights, repeating it seven times;
then the wise man, constantly reciting this hymn, should resort to the medicinal herb.
One should announce, "Come here from the field of the enemy";
having sacrificed to Varuṇa in one's own field, one obtains the plants that destroy the enemy.
One who desires rain should approach Bṛhaspati with restrained diet,
provided with an offering of milk-rice and accompanied by burnt oblations.
One desiring rain should employ the hymn beginning with "O Bṛhaspati, Lord" (RgV 4.1.5a).
By paying homage to Parjanya as well, one obtains auspicious rain.
But everywhere, supreme peace is to be known; the seer is Apratiratha.
To whatever place he may go, even against an enemy, once he has been consecrated with this mantra.
RgV_4.2.(7a): One should not turn back without having conquered, for the power of Brahman is supreme.
RgV_4.2.(7b): One should recite this with all desires for the fulfillment of all desires.
One should employ this for a king who has set out for battle;
he conquers all enemies and is not defeated by others.
This is a blessing for one's safety on the road; it protects from thieves wandering upon the path, and from all beings, serpents, and piśācas.
One who desires offspring, being pure, should recite the hymn addressed to Bhūtāṃśa Kāśyapa;
he quickly obtains suitable progeny—of this there is no doubt.
A twice-born man should win over the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, with an offering of cooked food from a pot;
indeed, having offered oblations with this very hymn, he should consecrate his horses with it.
Milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, meat, boiled rice, curd, and parched grain flour;
likewise, boiled beans, barley-meal, and various kinds of fruits.
Having gathered together various maternal offerings— pure fragrances, foods and drinks,
as well as what is to be chewed, what is to be eaten, and what is to be drunk— at the rising of the sun.
One should practice the *bhūtāṃśa* [offering] as long as the sun has not set;
once midnight has passed, one should then offer it to the two Aśvins.
One shall obtain a son who is long-lived, handsome, and full of splendor;
and he who constantly practices this portion of the Bhūtas shall always be endowed with beauty.
The wise one should know that this seer is Sārvakāmin;
one who is firm in his vow should mutter the hymn beginning with "na vā u devāḥ."
He finds food everywhere wherever he may resort— he who, being discerning, considers his self to be afflicted by evil.

Having become self-restrained, he should mutter [the hymns] so that he may consider himself lightened of sin. One who desires eloquence should approach Speech, offering oblations while quickly muttering these [verses].
By reciting "I [go] with the Rudras" (RgV 1.114.1), one becomes eloquent and honored;
by muttering the eight-verse hymn beginning with "Not him" (RgV 2.27), which is dedicated to the Viśvedevas, the sage [attains these qualities].
Having destroyed all impurity, they dwell together with all the gods;
one who is pure and has observed his vows should always take refuge in the Night at night.
He who should desire, "May I not be born again in wombs," should mentally recite the verse beginning with "rātrī" a thousand times during the nights.
RgV_4.4.(22a): He should sacrifice with cooked food every night and day at night.
RgV_4.4.(22b): Being righteous, he should remain seated at night with his mind fixed on that [deity], and stand during the day.
After a year has passed, an oblation of caru prepared in milk is prescribed;
indeed, by means of this, a thousandfold offering is ordained to be performed during the day.
One should offer oblations at night during the first part of the night, being fully concentrated;
and during the day, the necessary duties should be performed in the shade, away from the heat of the sun's rays.
Thus, with a self composed through restraint, one should mentally recite this hymn;
then, in the third year, one should prepare a sacrificial pap (caru) with clarified butter.
Then the boon-granting goddess Night becomes his companion;
he addresses that boon-granting goddess who has come of her own accord.
"O child, the time for your departure will come— whether in a year, a season, a month, this very day, or even at this very moment," [said] the affectionate mother.
By merely reciting the *Rātrisūkta*, one attains that state;
one does not enter a womb again and is liberated from all sins.
A twice-born man should recite "O Agni, my splendor" (RgV 4.6.29a) while seeking all desires;
by offering clarified butter with this very verse, he shall attain all his desires.
One who is firm in his vows should constantly recite: "That which they fashion... (RgV 4.6.30a).
Neither sorcery (*kṛtyā*) nor the malevolent spells of those intent on harm shall injure him. (RgV 4.6.30b)
That which those who know it perform by means of the Aṅgiras-kalpa,
he repels all of that by means of the Praty-aṅgiras-kalpa.
But the wise one who knows the *pratyaṅgirasa* shall never come to harm;
neither intentional nor unintentional spells shall ever injure him anywhere.
Whether done unknowingly or knowingly, by one who is angry or by one who is resentful—
whether it be an insult or an evil word— the sin does not cling to one who knows that [truth].
In this very way, one should constantly recite [this hymn] to the Seer for the sake of well-being;
the Seer himself declared this to be the expiation for all transgressions.
One should always recite this seer’s verse at the settlement of stationary objects, as well as in cities, villages, and houses.
The wise man should have a three-stranded amulet made of gold;
it was then offered by that seer with a thousand oblations.
One should fasten it upon the head, or on the neck, or else upon the chest;
neither known nor unknown spells shall harm him.
With this very hymn, a wise man should have a gem made that is reddish like the blood of kings; the consecration mantra should be recited for that same duration.
In battles, one should consecrate with mantras the tops of banners, musical instruments,
seats, beds, and various kinds of vehicles.
As that seer of the Aṅgiras lineage himself was performing the malevolent rite,
he countered all of it by means of the *Pratyaṅgirasa* ritual procedure.
One should perform sorcery against non-human beings while muttering this hymn of *kṛtyā*;
one is liberated from every kind of misfortune—how much more so, then, from fear of humans?
If a seer should be an ascetic, self-restrained, self-controlled, and a practitioner [of yoga], he, with a tranquil soul, overcomes everything; for asceticism is indeed a very great power.
This great hymn of Dakṣāyaṇa bestows long life, vitality, and splendor.
Upon obtaining an ornament or gold, one should recite the Dakṣāyaṇa hymn.
One who is intent on yoga should mutter and offer oblations with the mantra: "The non-existent did not exist. He thus acquires attained prosperity and partakes of abundant food.
One attains union with Prajāpati in twelve years;
moreover, one who is afflicted by illness should mutter the hymn "uta devāḥ" while remaining firm in his vows.
Having placed a jar of clarified butter, one should then offer oblations into the Jātavedas fire.
One should cause the residue from the jar to be deposited in another vessel made of bell-metal.
He who has sufficient food but does not eat it himself should prepare this [offering].
Having anointed his limbs with that clarified butter (*ājya*), he may slowly partake of his portion of food.

Even for one afflicted by disease, having anointed his body with this very [substance], he should recite this [hymn]. Even for those suffering from indigestion, he should anoint them; by that, they indeed become well.
One desiring wealth should employ the hymn beginning with "agne acchā vada" (RgV 4.10).
Restrained, having offered oblations of clarified butter, he should then recite it ten thousand times.
One should offer ten sets of ten fuel-sticks made of *khadira* wood;
by doing so ten times together with his wife, he thrives with the increase of wealth.
One who desires wealth should offer oblations with wood from the *bilva*, *udumbara*, *pālāśa*, and *rauhītaka* trees; thus he prospers through the increase of riches.
One who eats only once every half-month should offer oblations of fuel from the *vaibhītaka* tree and wood from the *bilva* tree.
At the conclusion of that rite, one should employ this hymn with a mind full of hatred toward an enemy.
Having slain the wealthy enemy, one obtains wealth from the foe;
or else, for one who desires the increase of riches and wealth, there should be only the recitation of prayers.
When there is danger from fire, one should recite the verse, "O Agni, this singer... (RgV 4.11).
Having gratified the fire according to the prescribed rite with milk, curd, ghee, and other offerings...
Having gone to the four directions as far as he wishes to drink himself,
he should pour out this water in a continuous stream.
Having become like a deep pool, [one should obtain] the medicine from Agni from nearby;
having gone to the forest, one should purchase the *pāṭhā* plant for a handful of barley.
RgV 4.11 (57a): If you belong to Soma, O gentle one, I purchase you from Soma as a plant.
RgV 4.11 (57b): Or if you belong to Varuṇa, I purchase you from Varuṇa. Thus [I say].
Whether from the Vasus, or from the Rudras, or again from the Ādityas—
since you belong to the Viśvedevas, I purchase you from all of them.
Having first cast *sumanasa* flowers together with the medicinal herb and the creeper,
he takes up its potency for whatever rite he is about to perform.
One should place that [plant] in the midst of the other herbs, suspended in the air;
however, this same rule shall apply everywhere for the gathering of the herbs.
Reciting, "One should cause this reading to be uprooted," one should do so here;
and in the morning, one should have it ground by a celibate student (brahmacārin) in the assembly.
In the absence of that [fire], one who observes the vow— whether a maiden or a Brāhmaṇa—
should, being pure in the morning, drink three times from it after it has been consecrated with ghee.
By reciting this hymn, beginning with the verse "imām," one hundred times or at least ten times,
she repels her rival wife, and her husband thinks exceedingly highly of her.
The husband, having recited this over her, should indeed drink it with milk for seven nights; thus he repels his rivals.
She who desires to conquer her husband by means of the recitation of root-mantras or other such practices sinks into hell,
for she belongs neither to this world nor to the realm of Yama.
Even medicinal powders and roots, when applied in the wrong manner, may destroy a person; therefore, one should not act otherwise.
She who speaks kindly to her husband, whose husband is her ultimate refuge,
and whose speech is sweet— this is the great means of winning over her husband.
Having obtained a beloved husband, she should indeed drink this medicinal herb—
one who speaks kindly, is devoted to dharma, is a lawful wife, and is beyond reproach.
He who, out of delusion, would despise her—they call him the lowest of men.
One should mutter this hymn repeatedly in the forests, saying, "O Araṇyānī! in the wilderness.
Having paid homage to Araṇyānī, he is released from the forest;
one who desires faith, being composed, should constantly recite the hymn of faith.
Everywhere he obtains faith, as well as intelligence and eloquent speech;
having approached the two Brāhmī hymns, he should recite them with his vows firmly restrained.
One should drink that [milk] according to one's capacity; within three days, one attains success.
One should take *śaṅkhapuṣpī* with milk and the flowers of *brāhmī* with clarified butter.
RgV 4.14 (73a): Having consecrated the *śatāvarī* plant with milk, water, or ghee, one should drink it—one portion at a time—for three days while reciting these two hymns. (73b)
One finds faith, intelligence, memory, nourishment, strength, and fortune;
one attains supreme success and enjoys a long life.
Alternatively, one may meditate upon this hymn with the mind and thereby attain success;
for the hymn "śāma itthā," which slays rivals, is for one desiring victory in battle.
It should be employed by one who is pure; one should offer oblations therein for the sake of success. Alternatively, it may simply be recited by one who is about to enter into battle.
RgV 4.15 (77a): "Śāma itthā"—he who would ward off all enemies;
(77b): for the sake of destroying misfortune, one should constantly recite the Śirimbiṭa hymn.
Having taken a branch of the Apāmārga plant together with Darbha grass and other creepers,
one should constantly purify oneself, both from below and above.
And with this [hymn], one should offer clarified butter ten times ten thousand times;
within three days, one drives away misfortune that has persisted for a hundred years from the body.
One performing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow should mutter this hymn, which brings about success;
it drives away misfortune from the body even if it has persisted for a thousand years.
One who has been seized by *yakṣman* (consumption), having taken darbha grass and touching [the patient], should mutter:
"I release you with an oblation. Thus he drives away the *yakṣman*.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the kindled fire according to the prescribed rule;
one should pour the remnants of the offering into the clarified butter and drink the milk with those remnants.
One should cause clarified butter and powder to be placed there in a vessel for mixing;
therein his food and his drink shall be consecrated with mantras.
Having ground pieces of *khadira* wood into powder and mixing them with water, one should purify the essence of the *iṣu* plants;
then one should drink it together with honey and clarified butter.
One should employ the mantra "I release you with oblation" (RV 4.16) in each respective instance;
by that ritual act, they draw the consumption-disease (yakṣma) away from the body.

If the fetus of a woman should die, one should offer an oblation into the fire with clarified butter according to the prescribed rule, reciting the mantra: "Agni, in harmony with the Brahman. (RgV 4.17.86ab)
Having anointed her with the remainder of the clarified butter (ājya), she shall then give birth;
indeed, by drinking that remainder of the clarified butter, she gives birth to a living child.

If those born [to him] should die, having prepared consecrated clarified butter (ājya), he should offer it with the mantra "Agni by means of the Brahman. He should pour the remnants of the oblation (sampāta) into the amulet.
One should place the gem upon a triple-stranded thread together with a cloth;
there, it should be wrapped with a shoot from a *nyagrodha* tree, encircled by white and red [threads].
Having consecrated him with ten thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī according to the prescribed rule,
he should likewise be praised by the Brahman priest with ten thousand *sampāta* offerings and the [Sāvitrī] hymn.
And after the Sāvitrī verse, the consecration is performed in the same manner;
one should recite over the consecrated amulet all the *svastyayana* (auspicious) hymns.
A woman who is pregnant, being pure and self-controlled, should wear this gem upon her head;
she should fasten it on during the third month of her pregnancy.
As a woman in her season, as a cow with her calf, so may she dwell in autumn rich in flowers—
abounding in water and grass, together with her calf that drinks its fill.
One should place that amulet around the neck of the newborn child,
having first set aside the remainder of the clarified butter and having anointed the boy with it.
By performing oblations with the *svastyayana* hymns, one gives birth to either a son or a daughter;
after a year has passed, the *svastyayana* rite is prescribed once again.
Before offering the breast, one should have him drink from it while reciting the Śraddhā-hymn;
and likewise, he should offer him ground rice-mash made of *vrīhi* grain while reciting the Medhā-hymn.
The wise man, by means of that gold mixed with honey, becomes wise;
he shall live for a hundred years and shall not die before his full span of life.
After six months from that time, he shall simply remember [the mantra];
then the twice-born man, having prepared clarified butter, should offer it with the mantra, "To the two eyes, thee. (RgV 4.19.98ab)
Then, with his hand smeared with clarified butter, he should touch his head;
he should also touch his ears, eyes, chin, and nostrils.

In this very way, by reciting [this hymn] constantly, one is liberated from consumption (*yakṣman*). One should perform the destruction of consumption according to the very ritual procedure previously described.
One should effect the destruction of the yakṣa through oblations and recitations;
one should recite the hymn beginning with "Apehi," being pure, for the destruction of bad dreams.
When a dove settles upon one, one should offer clarified butter with the hymn beginning "O gods, the dove" (RgV 10.165), for they know it to be a messenger of Yama.
One should employ the *sapatnaghna* hymn for recitation and oblation;
one who is firm in his vows should constantly recite the hymn beginning with "yenedam."
Through that, one attains concentration of mind and is not deluded at all.
One should mutter the mantra "Mayo-bhūr vātaḥ" for the well-being of cattle.
One who is concentrated in mind should offer barley grains smeared with ghee into a fire of dried cow-dung in the middle of a cattle-pen,
having prepared them with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
One should consecrate a king under the asterisms of Tiṣya or Śravaṇa,
or under those of Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Soma, the Aśvins, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras.
Having offered oblations into the fire with verses containing the marks of royalty and with the Sāvitrī verse, being self-restrained and pure,
one should perform the *sampāta* offering with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*).
Having sprinkled him with the smooth juices of all herbs and with the water of rivers, while he was seated upon a throne covered with a tiger skin; RgV_4.21.(108b).
Standing facing him, one should say: "Be victorious over this earth!
O King, may your entire dharma increase as you protect the subjects."
"May you increase for the sake of glory, nourishment, victory, and prosperity.
May there be kings in your lineage. Then one should recite the *Apratiratha* hymn.
There should be a tiger skin, and the fuel-sticks should be made of *udumbara* wood;
having sprinkled him with water, one should thus consecrate the drums with mantras.
May the Vasus consecrate you in the eastern quarter for the sake of splendor;
may the Rudras consecrate you in the southern quarter for the sake of prosperity.
May the Ādityas consecrate you in the western quarter for the sake of nourishment;
may the Viśvedevas consecrate you in the northern quarter for the sake of excellence.
Having consecrated the king and greeted him with blessings, he should then address him with the mantra: "I have brought you within [my] heart."
One should constantly recite "pataṅgam" (RgV 4.22), which pierces ignorance;
for this indeed pierces illusion and subdues all illusions.
By this [mantra], one may ward off the illusion of Śambara or Indra’s net;
by this, one also subdues the illusions of invisible beings.

One who is observant of her vows should mutter the hymn beginning with "tyam ū ṣu" as a prayer for well-being. If a woman who has reached menopause should see a flower but does not conceive, [she should perform this rite].
"Viṣṇu has stirred the womb; having touched the womb, he should then mutter:
'May the great protection of the three be ours'—this one should mutter for a safe journey on the road. (RgV 4.23)

One should recite the hymn to Agni (RgV 4.23) against one who hates and the object of hatred, as a means of counteracting that enmity. Furthermore, by means of the hymn "āyam gauḥ" and all the verses of the Sārparājñī, one overcomes all [hostile forces].
One should indeed recite the *aghamarṣaṇa*, which is the purifier among purifiers;
and whoever, having entered the waters, should recite this three times with a well-composed mind.
Manu has declared that it is like the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice;
for the horse sacrifice is the sovereign of rituals, the dispeller of all evil.
Likewise, the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn is the dispeller of all sins;
Śaunaka says that it is the "Nairhastya," which shatters armies.
The seer Śaunaka, however, considers this to be meditable by the mind:
"O Bull, you gather together [the fuel] for the great act of establishing brotherhood."
One should employ this [mantra] when there is a division among kinsmen; they shall never be divided again.
But once a division has occurred, one should mutter this "Reconciliation" mantra which effects a union.
There shall be no further division where one constantly recites this:
"We choose that peace and well-being"—this one should recite for the sake of a safe journey.
The Mahānāmnī verses are the Supreme Brahman, the pure, eternal light. The Sapatnaghnīs and the Puṇyās are also recorded as the supreme Pāvamānī hymns.
One desiring rain should recite these eternal verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and the *vyāhṛtis*, starting from the hymn of Madhucchandas.
The hymns at the end [of the Ṛgveda] are the Mahānāmnīs; that collection is remembered as the Immortal (Amṛtā).
By means of this collection, the gods attained immortality in the past.
One who, being pure, recites this constantly attains immortality. Right here, however, one should insert the *pitṛ-sūktas* many times in the middle.
One should know that as the *pitryā* *saṃhitā*; by means of it, one gratifies the ancestors. In this very same way, having brought [the syllables] together, it becomes the *vāsavī* *saṃhitā*.
One who knows the law should perform the pacification of the dwelling site— whether it be dedicated to Rudra, Āditya, the Viśvedevas, or whichever deity one desires— in the center of the cow-pen.
One should scatter flowers, perfumes, garlands from trees, as well as medicinal herbs,
and likewise all kinds of grain, over the entire site.
In this rite, one should worship Vāstoṣpati and Bṛhaspati with milk-rice (pāyasa);
and one should offer oblations in each direction with leaves of the Udumbara and Palāśa trees.
Sūrya, Vāyu, Yama, the Pitṛs, Varuṇa, Nirṛti,
as well as Soma and Mahendra— these are indeed remembered as the deities in the [eight] directions.
One should give gifts to the Brahmins; it brings auspiciousness to the dwelling site. Indeed, this should be performed annually by the householder in his home.
If this is so, then even though other similar [deities] have not been mentioned,
such as Agni, Indra, Vāyu, Sūrya, and other gods—
Whichever deity one might run toward,
desiring to propitiate, [one should do so] with a suitable hymn according to the purpose as directed.
The direct perception of the seers (*ṛṣi*) through their vision of mantras is accepted as established;
in all cases, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or wealth for the successful accomplishment of the rite.
Śaunaka maintains that there is no ritual action whatsoever that is devoid of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);
for even a gift equal to a full vessel may suffice, provided it is given according to one's ability.
Therefore, even a very small sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given for the successful completion of the rite. One should give eleven bulls, or whatever else by which the teacher is satisfied;
and the gift of sacred knowledge (*brahma-dāna*) is bestowed upon one who knows the Dharma and speaks the truth.
This supreme Brahman is secret, purifying, and wonderful.
It must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor to one who has no son, nor to one who lacks austerity.
It must not be given to one who has not resided [as a student] for a year, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is unfriendly.
For men who are bereft of fortune and ignorant of the ritual application of the Ṛgveda,
this Ṛgveda— the wish-fulfilling tree— does not yield its fruit at all.
Like a dwelling filled with jewels,
the Ṛgveda appears before me.
Without the lamp of the *Ṛgvidhāna*, it does not shine at all.
Like a mine of jewels, the sublime Ṛgveda is exceedingly difficult to traverse.
Without the great boat of the *Ṛgvidhāna*, it does not bestow fruit at all.

The Ṛgveda is the abode of all jewels and the temple of Brahman. For this Ṛgveda, if merely recited by men without its ritual application (ṛgvidhāna), becomes fruitless; therefore, it should be studied with diligent effort.
He who understands the *Ṛgvidhāna*, which explains the true meaning of the hymns (*sūkta*),
becomes one whose mind is blossoming through the grace of the *Ṛgveda*.
The performance of the *Ṛgvidhāna* rites is the root of longevity and prosperity, the destroyer of all impurities,
and the supreme bringer of radiant fame.
The twice-born who knows the Ṛgveda as it is joined with the Ṛgvidhāna shall certainly become the refuge for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
The first among the Vedas,
the lord who is the treasury of Āyurveda,
is exceedingly delighted by the constant practice of the *Ṛgvidhāna*.
The destruction of enemies, satisfaction of the mind, and reunion with kinsmen— the Ṛgveda,
when constantly propitiated according to the Ṛgvidhāna, grants these.
He who knows the Ṛgveda with its auxiliary limbs and is always devoted to the Ṛgvidhāna— whatever he desires shall be fulfilled for him,
even more than his heart's wish.
Regarding lineage, birth, character, wisdom, and even exertion,
they desire the fulfillment of one's conduct through a thorough mastery of the *Ṛgvidhāna*.
All the deities become pleased and all prosperities are attained;
the anxieties of those who constantly recite the ritual rules of the Ṛgveda perish.
Just as I have seen the manuscript, so has it been written by me.
Whether it be correct or incorrect, no fault should be attributed to me.
He who, having transcribed the work of the Ṛṣis, bestows it upon Brāhmaṇas, [attains great merit].
His ancestors dwell in Vaikuṇṭha for as many years as there are syllables [in the work].
With a broken back, waist, and neck, his fist clenched and face turned downward, he has written this with great hardship; therefore, one should preserve it with diligent effort.
"Guard it from oil; guard it from water; guard it from loose binding;
guard it when it has fallen into another's hand—thus speaks the book."
